M67.look: From Acubens, the star at the bottom of Cancer south of the Beehive, drift about two degrees west to a misty patch peppered with a handful of faint stars. The sky around it is thin in stars, well away from the band of the Milky Way.
M67.answer: Its orbit lifted it out of harm's way: M67, about 2,731 light-years from us, rides high above the thin middle layer of the disk, where the massive gas clouds and spiral arms that tear clusters apart are rare. Families that stay in the busy midplane, the Sun's own among them, dissolve long before they reach such an age.
M67.story: Astronomers know its orbit because Gaia measures its motion across the sky and spectra measure its speed toward us. With the galaxy's gravity, those wind into a path that carries the cluster well above and below the midplane. Some have even asked whether the Sun was born here, since the two are so alike in age and makeup, but the Sun's orbit is too flat to have come from there.

M7.beat: Our arm, in front of the center
M7.question: What is the rich glow behind Ptolemy's Cluster?
M7.why: Ptolemy's Cluster is one of the nearest clusters in the direction of the galaxy's center, a foreground family set against some of the deepest star fields in the sky.
M7.look: From Shaula, the Scorpion's stinger, go about five degrees north-east. The cluster spreads dozens of stars over more than a degree, and behind them the Milky Way is so dense it looks like fine sand, with dark notches of dust cutting into it.
M7.answer: The glow behind it is the inner galaxy, for the cluster is a near neighbor in our own arm while the background stars lie thousands of light-years beyond it. They pile up along a line of sight that crosses the next arm on its way toward the hub. In one field you see our neighborhood and, behind it, a crowd of stars much closer to the center than we are.
M7.story: Ptolemy's Cluster is near enough that Gaia measures the shift of its bright members directly, so its place in front of the glow is a matter of geometry rather than inference. The stars behind it are mostly too faint and too far for single parallaxes, and their depths come instead from star counts and from stars of known brightness.

M79.question: What is a globular cluster doing in the winter sky, opposite the galaxy's center?
M79.why: M79 is a small, round glow below Orion's feet, and it lies almost as far from the crowd of globulars as it can get.
M79.look: Go to Lepus, the Hare, below Orion. From Nihal (β Leporis) move about four degrees south; M79 looks like a small, round, slightly fuzzy star that will not focus to a point.
M79.answer: It may be an immigrant: the orbit of M79 ties it to a smaller galaxy that the Milky Way swallowed long ago, though which one is still debated. Part of the halo was built this way, from the clusters and stars of devoured neighbors, so the galaxy you live in is partly made of others.
M79.story: A swallowed galaxy's stars spread across the sky within a few orbits, but each keeps the energy and the spin around the center that it had when it arrived. Astronomers sort clusters by those two quantities, and clusters that came in together still bunch up on such a chart billions of years later. The boundaries between the groups are blurry, though, and some clusters fit more than one.

M8.question: How far is it to the next spiral arm toward the center?
M8.why: The Lagoon is the brightest nursery of the Sagittarius Milky Way, and nurseries are the lamps astronomers use to find spiral arms.
M8.look: About six degrees north of the tip of the Teapot's spout, find a misty knot in the Milky Way. Binoculars show an oval gray glow split by a dark lane, with a ragged young cluster on one side, a glow from well beyond our own arm.
M8.answer: The next arm in lies a few thousand light-years off, as far as the Lagoon and the young cluster beside it, and the Omega and Eagle nebulae nearby sit at broadly similar depths. Between our arm and this one lies a gap where far fewer nurseries glow, and beyond it the Sagittarius arm curves around the galaxy on the inner side of ours.
M8.story: The Lagoon's distance comes from Gaia's parallaxes of the young stars in its cluster, which is how astronomers know it sits beyond our own arm. The space between arms is not empty of stars, only of the young bright ones: older stars fill the whole disk fairly evenly, while new ones switch on where an arm gathers the gas.

M81.question: Why are galaxies easiest to find far from the Milky Way's band?
M81.why: Bode's Galaxy is one of the brightest galaxies beyond our own little family, and it shines in the Great Bear, well away from the band.
M81.look: Extend the line from Phecda through Dubhe by the same distance again, near the faint star 24 Ursae Majoris. Brace the binoculars: Bode's Galaxy is an oval haze with a starlike core, and the Cigar Galaxy shares the field as a thin silvery streak.
M81.answer: Away from the band you look out of our dusty disk instead of through it: toward the band, the same dust that splits the Milky Way into dark lanes hides almost every galaxy behind it. Here the view is clear, and even a spiral as distant as Bode's Galaxy, about 11.8 million light-years away, comes through as a soft oval in binoculars.
M81.story: Astronomers call the band's hiding effect the zone of avoidance: in old catalogs, galaxies seemed to shun a strip along the Milky Way, until infrared and radio surveys found them there, dimmed by dust rather than absent. Ursa Major lies far from that strip, which is why its galaxies show up even in binoculars.

M83.question: What would our galaxy look like from directly above its disk?
M83.why: The Southern Pinwheel is a barred spiral seen almost face-on, the view of a galaxy that we can never have of our own.
M83.look: Catch it due south, well below Spica: the Southern Pinwheel lies about 7° south-south-east of γ Hydrae, toward the border with Centaurus, so use a chart for the last hop. In 10×50s it is a soft, round glow with a brighter middle.
M83.answer: From above, our galaxy would look something like the Southern Pinwheel: a bright central bar with arms winding out from its ends, strung with young clusters and glowing nurseries like the ones that line our own arm. The Milky Way has a bar of its own across its middle, and somewhere out in one of its arms, between the bright lanes, sits the Sun.
M83.story: Our own galaxy's bar was found from inside, because stars near its center move as a bar would make them move. Infrared counts of stars toward the bulge are lopsided too, more on one side than the other, as if a long bar were tilted toward us. Seen face-on, the Southern Pinwheel's bar and arms are the pattern those clues describe.

M92.question: How old is the oldest layer of our galaxy?
M92.why: M92 looks like a smaller, fainter Great Hercules Cluster, but its stars are even poorer in heavy elements, and among the oldest anyone has dated.
M92.look: From π Herculis, the Keystone's north-east corner, go about 6° north to M92, an almost starlike center wrapped in a small glow. Flip back and forth between it and the Hercules cluster to compare them.
M92.answer: The halo is older than anything else in the galaxy, and M92 shows it: its age comes out between about 12.75 and 13.8 billion years, depending on the method. The disk you see along the band, with its nurseries and young families, is the younger part of the galaxy, built inside a halo that was already ancient.
M92.story: Dated with the same method, the globulars poorest in heavy elements, M92 among them, share a single great age within the errors, while richer clusters spread toward younger ages by up to a couple of billion years. Astronomers read the first group as the galaxy's own earliest generation and many of the younger ones as later arrivals, brought in by small galaxies the Milky Way swallowed.

M94.question: Is most of our own galaxy's mass in the stars we can see?
M94.why: M94 is one of the easier galaxies near Cor Caroli, and the way it spins puts the weight of our own galaxy in a new light.
M94.look: From Cor Caroli, below the Big Dipper's handle, move about three degrees north. M94's compact, bright core makes it one of the easier galaxies here, a fuzzy star wrapped in a soft halo.
M94.answer: Most of our galaxy's mass is not in the stars you can see, because the Milky Way is one of the many spirals whose outskirts spin too fast. The stars and gas along the band are only the bright part of a far heavier, invisible halo that wraps the disk and the globulars alike. M94, which seems to need so little dark matter, is the exception that keeps astronomers testing the rule.
M94.story: Weighing our own galaxy is harder than weighing M94, because we ride along inside the disk we are trying to measure. Astronomers combine the Sun's speed around the center, about two hundred thirty kilometers every second, with the motions of globular clusters and small companion galaxies far out in the halo. The total comes to somewhere around a trillion Suns.

MWF-CygnusRift.question: Why does a dark lane run down the middle of the summer Milky Way?
MWF-CygnusRift.why: The Cygnus Rift splits the summer band lengthwise, and its shape is a clue to how dust is spread through the whole disk.
MWF-CygnusRift.look: Under a dark sky, follow the Milky Way from Deneb past Sadr toward Albireo, where a dark band splits it into two streams. Sweep binoculars slowly across the boundary, and the star-rich fields give way to dim, nearly empty ones.
MWF-CygnusRift.answer: The dust lies in a thin sheet along the middle of the disk, and from inside that sheet we see it edge-on as a lane, here a chain of cold clouds a couple of thousand light-years away. From outside, our galaxy would show the same dark stripe that edge-on spiral galaxies show, and behind the stripe its arms go on making stars.
MWF-CygnusRift.story: Dust is confined even more tightly than the stars: most of it lies within a few hundred light-years above or below the midplane, a thinner layer than the one that holds the disk's stars. Astronomers measured that thickness by checking how much stars at different heights are reddened: stars a few hundred light-years up shine through almost clean, while stars as far off along the midplane are badly dimmed.

Mel111.question: What lies straight up, out of the plane of our galaxy?
Mel111.why: The Coma Star Cluster is one of the nearest star families, and by chance it sits almost exactly where the view points out of the disk, so it is the foreground for everything that way.
Mel111.look: Look between Denebola and Cor Caroli for a faint glittery patch, and let binoculars spread it into a loose sprawl of white stars. Around it the background is noticeably sparse compared with any stretch of the Milky Way, and that sparseness is the clue.
Mel111.answer: Very little of our galaxy lies that way, only the thin outskirts of the disk and the scattered old clusters of the halo. This cluster, about 278 light-years away, sits close to the north pole of the Milky Way's disk. Beyond that the line of sight leaves home, which is why Coma and neighboring Virgo are thick with faint galaxies.
Mel111.story: The galaxy's north pole sits in Coma Berenices, a point found by tracing the Milky Way's midline around the whole sky and taking the spot a quarter-turn from it in every direction. Astronomers measure every star's height above the disk from that grid, the way a surveyor measures from sea level.

Mel20.question: Is the Sun's neighborhood still turning out young star families?
Mel20.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster is one of the nearest young star families to the Sun, and it is still rich in the kind of stars that cannot be old.
Mel20.look: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too wide for most telescopes but just right for binoculars. Blue-white stars burn out fast, so a crowd of them is a young crowd.
Mel20.answer: Our neighborhood made this family only recently, since the Alpha Persei Cluster, about 566 light-years away, still holds hot blue-white members that burn through their fuel quickly. Stars were being born in our part of the disk not long ago by a galaxy's standards. A disk that still makes families around us is a sign that the Sun lives inside a spiral arm, and beyond Perseus, thousands of light-years farther in the same direction, lies the next one.
Mel20.story: Families this young are not scattered evenly around the Sun: Gaia's census of young stars within a few thousand light-years shows them gathered into long lanes and waves, and the Alpha Persei Cluster sits on one of them. Tracing those lanes is how astronomers outline the arm the Sun lives in.

NGC104.beat: The halo's edge, beside another galaxy
NGC104.question: Is 47 Tucanae part of the Small Magellanic Cloud right beside it?
NGC104.why: 47 Tucanae and the Small Magellanic Cloud share a single binocular view, and the pair is the best place in the sky to see where our galaxy ends.
NGC104.look: To the eye it is a fuzzy star at the edge of the Small Magellanic Cloud. Binoculars show a round glow brightening sharply to an intense core, and wide binoculars hold the cluster and the Cloud's edge in one view.
NGC104.answer: 47 Tucanae belongs to our own halo, while the Cloud behind it lies nearly fourteen times farther, a separate galaxy far outside ours. In one field you see the Milky Way's old outer swarm and, far behind it, the next galaxy over.
NGC104.story: Distance is one test of belonging and motion is another. Spectra show the Small Cloud receding from us at about a hundred and fifty kilometers per second, while 47 Tucanae drifts toward us at less than twenty. Whatever the two share on the sky, they are not traveling through space together.

NGC2244.beat: Deeper outward: star birth beyond the Sun
NGC2244.question: Does the galaxy still make stars farther from its center than the Sun?
NGC2244.why: The Rosette Cluster lies in Monoceros, on the side of the sky that faces away from the galaxy's center, and its stars are newborns.
NGC2244.look: Go about a third of the way from Betelgeuse to Procyon and drop slightly south into Monoceros. A small rectangle of stars stands out, one of them yellow-orange, and on a very dark night a faint ring of haze may show around the group, gas the young stars are still lighting.
NGC2244.answer: The galaxy still makes stars out here. The Rosette's young stars lie in a direction pointing away from the hub, so they sit farther from the center than the Sun, and the gas around them glows because they switched on so recently. The outer disk is thinner and quieter than the inner one, but its arms are still at work.
NGC2244.story: Radio maps show the disk's hydrogen reaching well beyond the Sun's orbit, thinning but not gone. Out there the disk also warps, bending up on one side of the galaxy and down on the other like the brim of a hat.

NGC2264.question: Where does our spiral arm go beyond Orion?
NGC2264.why: The Christmas Tree Cluster is a nursery a little deeper along the band than Orion's, so it shows which way our own arm runs.
NGC2264.look: Go a little under halfway from Betelgeuse to Procyon, then north into Monoceros. Bright S Monocerotis marks the trunk of an upside-down tree of fainter stars, a family still sitting in the cloud that made it.
NGC2264.answer: Our arm runs on through Monoceros: this cluster, about 2,280 light-years away, is still forming stars at the tip of its tree, which marks it as another working nursery of the same arm. Line up nurseries like it by their measured distances and the arm appears as a lane of young stars curving away from us through the winter sky.
NGC2264.story: The direction of the arm shows up when nurseries are plotted on a map seen from above: Orion's clouds, then the Christmas Tree's farther along, step outward on a gently curving line. Each distance comes from Gaia's parallaxes of the young stars themselves, so the curve is measured, not drawn by eye.

NGC2362.question: How far beyond Sirius does the Milky Way of Canis Major run?
NGC2362.why: The τ Canis Majoris Cluster is a tiny knot of young stars in the Great Dog's hindquarters, and its bright central star is not what it seems.
NGC2362.look: Find Wezen and Aludra in the Great Dog's hindquarters, south-east of Sirius. τ Canis Majoris sits about three degrees north of the point midway between them, looking slightly fuzzy, wrapped in a tiny knot of faint stars.
NGC2362.answer: It runs on for thousands of light-years, for this little cluster lies about 4,010 light-years away, nearly five hundred times as far as Sirius. τ Canis Majoris at its heart is a heavyweight that only looks ordinary because of that distance. The faint winter band here is made of suns as remote as this one, out on the side of the disk that faces away from the center.
NGC2362.story: The winter band is faint for two reasons that pull in opposite directions. Fewer stars lie out this way, since we look toward the disk's thinner outer regions, but less dust does too, so a cluster thousands of light-years off reaches us only a little dimmed. Here the disk is thin enough to see through, and only rare heavyweights like τ Canis Majoris stand out of it.

NGC253.question: What would our galaxy look like seen edge-on from far away?
NGC253.why: The Sculptor Galaxy is a big spiral seen nearly edge-on, the angle from which we see our own disk, only from outside instead of inside.
NGC253.look: Find Diphda, the brightest star of Cetus, and sweep about 7° almost due south for a faint elongated streak about the Moon's width long. From mid-northern latitudes it stays low, and averted vision lengthens it.
NGC253.answer: From a great distance, side-on, our galaxy would look like this thin streak, a bright, flattened spindle of stars that photographs show threaded with dark dust along its middle. Our Milky Way band is that same edge seen from inside it, which is why it wraps all the way around the sky.
NGC253.story: Its dark lanes are the same kind of dust that splits our own band, seen from far enough away to show its full sweep along the disk. In infrared light the dust glows and the stars behind it shine through, the same trick astronomers use to see through our own disk toward its center.

NGC3201.question: Why is NGC 3201 rushing away from us faster than any other globular?
NGC3201.why: NGC 3201 is a loose, soft glow in Vela, and its motion sets it apart from almost everything else in the galaxy.
NGC3201.look: In Vela, look for a soft, roundish glow about half the width of the full Moon, only slightly brighter toward the middle and much looser-looking than most globulars; moonlight easily washes it out.
NGC3201.answer: It circles the galaxy the wrong way: the disk, the Sun included, swings around the center in one direction, and NGC 3201 orbits against that flow, so much of its speed relative to us is our own motion added to its. A cluster on such an orbit has never shared the orderly spin of the disk, a member of the halo in the fullest sense.
NGC3201.story: Its strange orbit points to a strange origin. A cluster born in the spinning disk would share the disk's direction of rotation, so clusters that circle backward are thought to have arrived with small galaxies the Milky Way swallowed. Gaia's measurements of its motion tie this cluster to the debris of an ancient merger, though which one is still debated.

NGC3293.beat: The next arm in: a production line
NGC3293.question: How long does one stretch of spiral arm keep making stars?
NGC3293.why: The Gem Cluster and the young clusters inside the Carina Nebula came from one star-forming region at different times, so together they record a history.
NGC3293.look: From the bright heart of the Carina Nebula, move about two degrees north-west. Binoculars show a compact, bright clump much smaller than the Moon, a few stars resolved around a hazy center, standing in clear space with no glow around it.
NGC3293.answer: It goes on for well over ten million years: the Gem Cluster is roughly 15 million years old, while the nurseries beside it are still making stars, so this patch of the arm has turned gas into families batch after batch. A spiral arm is not one event but a long production line, and Carina is one of its busiest stretches.
NGC3293.story: Star birth in a giant cloud complex rarely happens all at once. The winds of one generation's heaviest stars, and later their supernovae, squeeze the gas around them and can set off the next batch. In Carina those generations run across the sky, from cleared clusters like this one to infant stars still hidden in dusty pillars.

NGC3372.beat: The next arm in, seen end-on
NGC3372.question: Why is the Milky Way in Carina so crowded with nurseries and clusters?
NGC3372.why: The Carina Nebula is the brightest nursery of the southern sky, and its setting tells as much as its glow.
NGC3372.look: Sweep the Milky Way between the Southern Cross and the False Cross, where the glow is plain to the eye. Binoculars show a bright, irregular haze cut by a dark notch of dust, with the orange point of Eta Carinae beside it and young clusters scattered all around.
NGC3372.answer: Here our line of sight runs along the next arm in rather than across it, so its nurseries and young clusters stack up one behind another, and the Carina Nebula is the grandest of them. The same arm, followed the other way around the sky, is the one you see glowing in Sagittarius.
NGC3372.story: Directions like this one, where the line of sight grazes an arm, show up in radio maps of the galaxy's gas as places where the signal suddenly strengthens, and astronomers call them arm tangents. They are among the most reliable markers of where the arms run, because they do not depend on any single distance.

NGC3532.question: How many spiral arms lie between the Wishing Well and the Carina Nebula?
NGC3532.why: The Wishing Well Cluster sits only a few degrees from the Carina Nebula, and the two look like neighbors until you ask how far each one is.
NGC3532.look: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east to an elongated swarm of dozens of stars in curving chains. Keep both in one sweep and compare: the cluster is crisp and resolved, the nebula a hazy glow set deeper in the band.
NGC3532.answer: You cross the gap between two arms. The Wishing Well lies about 1,540 light-years away in our own arm, while the Carina Nebula sits about five times farther, in the arm that runs inward of ours through Carina and Sagittarius. Looking toward Carina, a single sweep spans the space between two arms of the galaxy.
NGC3532.story: The Carina Nebula's distance comes from the expanding shell around Eta Carinae, and the Wishing Well's from Gaia's parallaxes of hundreds of members, two independent methods for two very different objects. Plotted on a map of the disk seen from above, distances like these are what reveal the lanes of the arms and the quieter gaps between them.

NGC457.beat: The next arm out, to the naked eye
NGC457.question: Can you see a single star in another spiral arm with your own eyes?
NGC457.why: The Owl Cluster's bright eye, φ Cassiopeiae, shows to the naked eye on a dark night, and whether it belongs to the cluster decides how far away that eye is.
NGC457.look: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find the bright star φ Cassiopeiae with a fainter partner beside it, and the faint spray of the Owl's wings trailing away from them. Then look at φ Cassiopeiae with the naked eye alone.
NGC457.answer: φ Cassiopeiae is probably just that, since Gaia's measurement puts it at the cluster's distance, out in the Perseus arm. That would make it one of the most luminous stars in the galaxy, bright enough to reach your naked eye across the gap between two arms. The case is not quite closed, which only makes that pinpoint more intriguing.
NGC457.story: Distance is not the only toll on this light, for the dust along this line of sight soaks up roughly three quarters of it on the way. A star still bright enough for the naked eye after crossing that much distance and that much dust would have to shine well over a hundred thousand times as brightly as the Sun.

NGC4755.beat: The next arm in, beside the dark
NGC4755.question: How can the Jewel Box sparkle right at the edge of the Coalsack's shadow?
NGC4755.why: The Jewel Box sits just outside the Coalsack's edge, and the two together show two depths of the disk in one field.
NGC4755.look: Start at Mimosa on the eastern arm of the Cross and nudge just over a degree south-east to a compact letter A of stars, one of them orange. Sweep a little south and the star fields fade into the Coalsack's darkness.
NGC4755.answer: The two are nowhere near each other: the Coalsack is a dust cloud about 500 light-years away, while the Jewel Box lies more than twelve times farther, in the next arm in. From here the young cluster just peeks out past the cloud's edge, one of the many lamps of the inner arm that the dust lets through.
NGC4755.story: Its distance comes from Gaia's parallaxes, averaged over hundreds of members, and from matching its hot stars against nearer young families. Both put it on the arm that runs inward of ours through Centaurus and Carina. Clusters as young as this one are the most trusted markers of an arm, because they have not had time to drift away from it.

NGC5128.beat: Beyond: a different kind of galaxy
NGC5128.question: Is every galaxy a flat spiral like the Milky Way?
NGC5128.why: Centaurus A is a faint oval glow a few degrees north of Omega Centauri, and it is built quite differently from our own galaxy.
NGC5128.look: Start at Omega Centauri and move about four and a half degrees north. Under a dark sky binoculars show a small, slightly oval glow that swells with averted vision.
NGC5128.answer: Centaurus A is a giant elliptical, a vast rounded swarm of stars rather than a thin spinning disk, and the nearest galaxy of its kind. Spirals like ours, with their arms and nurseries, are only one of the ways a galaxy can be built.
NGC5128.story: Giant ellipticals are thought to grow by mergers, and Centaurus A shows the evidence: a lane of dust and young stars cuts across its middle, the remains of a gas-rich spiral it swallowed. Our own galaxy has eaten only small neighbors so far, but its merger with Andromeda, billions of years from now, may leave something rather like this.

NGC5139.beat: The halo: a lost galaxy's heart
NGC5139.question: Could the grandest globular in our sky be what is left of another galaxy?
NGC5139.why: Omega Centauri is the biggest and brightest globular cluster of the Milky Way, and its stars do not follow the rules that ordinary globulars keep.
NGC5139.look: To the eye it is a fuzzy star in Centaurus that never sharpens. Binoculars turn it into a large, round glow brightening steadily toward the center, like a snowball, grainy at the edge under a dark sky.
NGC5139.answer: Omega Centauri, about 17,700 light-years from us, may well be just that. Its several generations of stars and its backward orbit around the galaxy fit the core of a small galaxy that merged with the young Milky Way and was stripped of everything but its dense heart. If so, the halo holds the remains of the galaxies ours has eaten, and Omega Centauri is the largest of them you can see by eye.
NGC5139.story: In 2019 astronomers sifting Gaia's measurements found a faint river of stars, named Fimbulthul, stretching across tens of degrees of the southern sky. Its stars share Omega Centauri's motion and, as later spectra showed, its unusual mix of chemistry. It is a tail pulled off the cluster by the Milky Way's tides, still tracing the orbit the cluster has followed for billions of years.

NGC6231.beat: The next arm in, behind our own
NGC6231.question: Which of the bright stars around NGC 6231 belong to the next spiral arm?
NGC6231.why: NGC 6231 is a compact knot of brilliant young stars at the tail of Scorpius, and the bright stars around it come from two very different depths.
NGC6231.look: Follow Scorpius's tail to the naked-eye pair ζ¹ and ζ² Scorpii, then go half a degree north to a compact knot of a dozen bright stars over fainter ones. Compare the two ζ stars: one orange, one pale.
NGC6231.answer: NGC 6231 and the paler ζ¹ do, both about 5,190 light-years away at the core of a group of hot young stars in the next arm in, while orange ζ² is a nearby giant in our own stretch of the disk. ζ¹ looks pale rather than blue because dust along that long road reddens its light, and a single glance here spans the gap between two spiral arms.
NGC6231.story: This cluster is the core of a sprawling association of hot young stars spread over a few hundred light-years along the next arm in. Associations like it are so young that they still sit where their birth clouds were, which makes them the brightest markers astronomers have for plotting where an arm runs.

NGC6397.beat: The halo, dated by its embers
NGC6397.question: How old is the galaxy's halo, judged by its dying embers?
NGC6397.why: NGC 6397 is one of the nearest globular clusters, a bright, ragged glow in Ara, close enough for Hubble to see its dimmest dead stars.
NGC6397.look: From β Arae, below Scorpius' tail, sweep about three degrees north-east to a bright, irregular glow with a concentrated core and a ragged halo. From mid-northern latitudes it barely clears the horizon, while from the southern hemisphere it is a highlight.
NGC6397.answer: The embers say about 11.5 billion years: the faintest white dwarfs Hubble found in NGC 6397 have been cooling that long, and fits to its living stars give an even older figure. The halo's clusters formed in the galaxy's first few billion years, and the disk is the younger structure that grew inside them.
NGC6397.story: NGC 6397 also carries a clock of a stranger kind, the rare element beryllium, made when cosmic rays from the galaxy's first exploding stars shattered atoms of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. Its amount built up steadily as time passed, and in 2004 astronomers used the beryllium in this cluster's stars to estimate that it formed only a few hundred million years after the galaxy's first stars.

NGC7000.question: What does a working stretch of our own spiral arm look like?
NGC7000.why: The North America Nebula is one of the nurseries of the Cygnus Milky Way, and it shows what our own arm is doing in our era rather than long ago.
NGC7000.look: Put Deneb at the edge of a wide field and look about 3° east. On a dark, transparent night the area looks slightly brighter than the surrounding Milky Way, with a sharper dark edge on its southern side. A nebula filter helps, and rich star fields should not be mistaken for the glow.
NGC7000.answer: A working stretch of arm looks much like this faint glow: a cloud of hydrogen about 2,640 light-years away, lit by hot young stars that have switched on inside it and still wrapped in lanes of dust. Glowing gas, fresh stars and dark dust together are the signature of a spiral arm, and from inside one, that mixture is what the band of Cygnus is made of.
NGC7000.story: Nurseries glow red in photographs because hydrogen gives off a deep red light when electrons fall back into atoms that ultraviolet starlight had torn apart. That color is how astronomers find nurseries across a galaxy. In face-on spirals the red knots line up along the arms like beads; in ours they crowd the band of Cygnus because we look along the arm.

NGC752.question: Why does an old cluster like NGC 752 sit so far from the Milky Way's band?
NGC752.why: NGC 752 is far older than the clusters strung along the band, and its position is a record of what time does to a star family's orbit.
NGC752.look: Start at the wide orange pair 56 Andromedae in southern Andromeda and look just north-east for a large, loose patch of faint, similar stars. Then notice where you are: the band of the Milky Way runs well to the north, through Cassiopeia and Perseus.
NGC752.answer: Time has pushed it there, because every passage near a massive cloud or through a spiral arm gives a cluster a small kick. Over more than a billion years those kicks have let NGC 752, about 1,414 light-years away, bob far above and below the thin layer where it was born. Young clusters hug the band and old ones wander, so a cluster's height above the plane is a rough clock of its age.
NGC752.story: Astronomers call this disk heating, and they measure it by comparing families and single stars of different ages. The spread of their up-and-down speeds grows steadily with age, so the oldest members of the disk bob highest above its midplane. This cluster's place far from the band, and the motion Gaia measures for it, fit that pattern.

NGC869.question: What lies across the quiet gap beyond our own spiral arm?
NGC869.why: The Double Cluster is one of the finest binocular sights of the northern sky, and it lies much farther away than its brightness suggests.
NGC869.look: Sweep from Cassiopeia's W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points, a few of them orange. Lower the binoculars and the naked eye still shows them as a hazy patch in the Milky Way.
NGC869.answer: The Perseus arm does, and the Double Cluster is its brightest landmark in our sky: these clusters belong to the next arm out from the center, across a gap where far fewer young stars shine. Past Perseus the disk thins toward its outer edge, so in this direction the rich clusters give out sooner than they do toward Sagittarius.
NGC869.story: The distance to the arm beyond the gap was one of the early triumphs of radio parallaxes. In 2006 a maser in a nursery in this part of the sky gave a distance by pure geometry, and it settled a long argument by showing that arm to be nearer than older estimates based on the speed of its gas. Gaia's distance to the Double Cluster now fits the same lane.

NGC884.beat: The next arm out: one burst
NGC884.question: How big a stretch of spiral arm can light up in one burst of star birth?
NGC884.why: χ Persei is the eastern twin of the Double Cluster, and its twin is only the start of its family.
NGC884.look: Keep both clusters in the field and compare: χ Persei is a little looser than h. Then sweep slowly around the pair at low power, where a sprinkling of bright stars spreads across the surrounding field.
NGC884.answer: A whole region of the arm can switch on together: both clusters and a wide halo of stars around them share one age, so a large patch of the Perseus arm formed its stars in a single burst. Bursts like this are how spiral arms light up, and seen from outside they would be the bright knots that mark an arm in a photograph of a galaxy.
NGC884.story: A burst that big needs a big cloud. A giant cloud usually turns only a few percent of its gas into stars, so two rich clusters and the scattered family around them point to a parent of hundreds of thousands of Suns' worth of gas. Clouds that heavy gather mostly where a spiral arm sweeps gas together.

SMC.beat: Beyond: the galaxy that measured ours
SMC.question: How did this little galaxy help map our own?
SMC.why: The Small Magellanic Cloud is a companion galaxy of the Milky Way, and in the story of finding our place it plays a surprising part.
SMC.look: Under a dark sky it looks like a small torn-off cloud; binoculars show a soft, uneven glow, brighter along one side, with 47 Tucanae and NGC 362, two globulars of our own halo, as fuzzy stars beside it.
SMC.answer: Leavitt's rule gave astronomers lamps of known power, and Harlow Shapley used that kind of yardstick to measure the distances of globular clusters and place the center of the galaxy far off in Sagittarius. The Cloud itself is one of the small companion galaxies that circle our own, near enough that its brightest stars could be timed one by one.
SMC.story: Leavitt's rule said only which Cepheids were truly brighter than others, not how bright any of them actually was, so the scale still floated free. In 1913 Ejnar Hertzsprung pinned it down from the slow drift of a dozen or so nearby Cepheids across the sky, and with that one fixed point the rule became a working yardstick.

STAR-Arcturus.question: Is every star near the Sun a local, or are some just passing through?
STAR-Arcturus.why: Arcturus is a near neighbor and one of the brightest stars of the sky, yet it does not move like the stars around it, and that difference opens a window on the galaxy's layers.
STAR-Arcturus.look: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle to Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes, and hold it in the field: its orange-gold is obvious. It sits far from the Milky Way's band, in a part of the sky that looks up and out of the disk rather than along it.
STAR-Arcturus.answer: Some are just passing through, and Arcturus is the brightest of them. It only happens to be crossing our neighborhood now, on an orbit that climbs higher above and below the disk's thin middle layer than the Sun ever goes. The galaxy is layered, a young thin disk inside an older, thicker one and an ancient halo around both, and the Sun belongs to the thin, young layer.
STAR-Arcturus.story: Arcturus does not travel alone, for dozens of other old stars share its unusual motion, a group astronomers call the Arcturus stream. They still debate whether it is debris from a small galaxy swallowed long ago or stars stirred into step by the bar at the galaxy's center. Either way, the Sun's neighborhood turns out to be a crossroads where stars of very different origins pass through.

STAR-Fomalhaut.beat: Home: looking out of the disk
STAR-Fomalhaut.question: Why does Fomalhaut stand so alone in its part of the sky?
STAR-Fomalhaut.why: Fomalhaut is a close neighbor of the Sun, but what makes it useful here is the empty sky around it.
STAR-Fomalhaut.look: Follow the west side of the Great Square of Pegasus about 45° south to Fomalhaut, the only bright star in that stretch. Sweep the binoculars around it and compare the sparse field with any patch of the Milky Way: far fewer faint stars fill the view.
STAR-Fomalhaut.answer: That part of the sky points well away from the plane of the disk, so after a few neighbors like Fomalhaut, about 25 light-years away, the line of sight runs out of stars quickly. Where the disk thins out the universe beyond opens up, and faint galaxies such as the Sculptor Galaxy hide not far to the east.
STAR-Fomalhaut.story: You can test this with nothing but a count: a binocular field near Fomalhaut holds only a fraction of the faint stars that crowd an equal field in Cygnus or Sagittarius. William Herschel made the same count with a telescope in the 1780s, sampling the sky field by field, and concluded that we live inside a flattened system of stars, the first rough map of the Milky Way.

STAR-Procyon.beat: Home: a neighbor at the band's edge
STAR-Procyon.question: Procyon sits at the edge of the winter Milky Way, so is it part of it?
STAR-Procyon.why: Procyon is one of the closest bright stars to the Sun, and it shines right beside the faint river of the winter Milky Way in Canis Minor and Monoceros.
STAR-Procyon.look: Find Procyon, the eastern corner of the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse. On a dark night the faint band of the winter Milky Way runs just to its west through Monoceros, a soft glow beside a brilliant point.
STAR-Procyon.answer: It belongs to the galaxy, as every star you see does, but not to that glow: Procyon is a close neighbor, while the band beside it is made of stars hundreds of times farther along the disk. Near stars lie all over our sky because we sit inside the disk's thickness, and only the distant ones pile up into a band.
STAR-Procyon.story: From Procyon our Sun would be a modest star, a little fainter than Polaris looks to us, in what we call Aquila, on the opposite side of the sky, and the Milky Way would look almost exactly as it does to us. A few light-years barely change the view of the galaxy, which is the clearest sign that the band is very far away and the neighbors are very close.

STAR-Sirius.question: Why are the Sun's nearest neighbors scattered all over the sky instead of along the band?
STAR-Sirius.why: Sirius outshines every other star of the night, yet it is not a giant beacon but a neighbor, and neighbors are the first clue to the shape of the thing we live in.
STAR-Sirius.look: Follow Orion's Belt down and to the left to Sirius, and park it near the edge of the field to tame the glare. Then lower the binoculars and notice where the brightest winter stars lie: Sirius, Procyon, Capella and Aldebaran are spread widely, some well away from the faint winter band of the Milky Way.
STAR-Sirius.answer: They are too close to show it: Sirius and the other near stars lie well within the thickness of the disk, so from where we sit they surround us in every direction, like the trees right around you in a forest. Only stars thousands of light-years off crowd into a band, and that crowding is the next clue to the shape of our galaxy.
STAR-Sirius.story: Astronomers have counted the Sun's neighbors with care, and out to about twenty light-years there are roughly a hundred known stars, most of them faint red dwarfs no eye can see. Infrared surveys still turn up new ones, cool brown dwarfs only a few light-years away. The neighbors we can see by eye are the rare bright exceptions, Sirius chief among them.

Stock2.beat: Our arm, next to the next arm
Stock2.question: Stock 2 and the Double Cluster share a sweep, but do they share an arm?
Stock2.why: Stock 2 is a big, loose family just north of the Double Cluster, and the pair is the clearest demonstration in the northern sky of how deep the band runs.
Stock2.look: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north until a large, loose group fills much of the view, the stick figure some call the Muscleman. Sweep back and forth between them: Stock 2's stars look bright and coarse, the Double Cluster's small and densely packed.
Stock2.answer: Stock 2 belongs to our own arm, while the Double Cluster lies across the gap in the Perseus arm, the next one out from the center. The difference in sparkle you just saw is the gap between two spiral arms, squeezed by perspective into two degrees of sky.
Stock2.story: Plot the young clusters in this part of the sky by their Gaia distances and they fall into two groups, one nearer than about three thousand light-years and one from about six to nine thousand, with few in between. Young families mark where arms are because they have had no time to wander away, so a stretch of distance with almost none of them is a landmark in its own right.

lenses.storyline: A bright Moon does not dim a single star. It adds a faint, even glow to every patch of sky, and whether you can still see something depends on how tightly it packs its light against that glow. The journey walks from the tightest packing to the loosest, starting with a single bright point whose color shrugs off the glare and then two points the glare cannot merge. Next comes a cluster whose faint members drop out while its bright ones remain. The walk ends on a glow of stars or gas too crowded or too far to split, the faintest kind of thing that still survives, though smaller than on a dark night. Each stop spreads its light more thinly than the last, so by the end you have seen exactly where moonlight starts to win, and why most nebulae and galaxies have vanished tonight or shrunk to their brightest hearts.

1>1: {next} is another single point, and like {prev} it holds its own against the glow however bright the Moon.
From {prev} to {next} you stay with lone points of light, each packing all its light into a spot the moonlit sky cannot match.
1>2: {prev} showed that a single point of light shrugs off the Moon; at {next} there is more than one point in the field, and the glow falls on each of them alike.
One bright point held its own at {prev}, and at {next} you have stars side by side, a chance to see how the glow treats each of them.
2>2: Beside {prev}, {next} is a fresh pair with its own mix of brightness and spacing, and its fainter star is the one to watch, because what the Moon takes from a pair is contrast, starting with the dimmer star.
{next} sets more stars side by side, and next to {prev} it shows that what decides each star's fate tonight is its brightness, not how close it sits to its neighbor.
1>3: From the single point of {prev} you jump to a crowd of them at {next}, and now the Moon has stars of many brightnesses to choose from.
{prev} was one star the Moon could not touch; {next} is a crowd of stars of every brightness, and the glare will not treat them all alike.
2>3: From the few points at {prev} to the crowd at {next}: a crowd is the same contest repeated star by star, and its faintest members are the first to lose.
The points at {prev} stayed apart; at {next} a whole crowd of them shares the field, and the Moon now gets to decide which of them you see.
3>3: A second crowd of stars waits at {next}, and beside {prev} it shows the Moon's cut falling in a different place, because the cut depends on how bright each member looks from here.
Moving from {prev} to {next} you meet another crowd of points, a fresh chance to see which members the glare spares and which it takes.
2>4: The stars at {prev} stayed clean points; {next} is light your binoculars cannot pull apart into points, a glow rather than a star, and that is the hardest kind of thing to keep in a moonlit sky.
After the crisp points at {prev}, {next} gives up on points altogether, and its light reaches you spread out as a glow.

{prev} was a crowd you could count; {next} is light your binoculars mostly cannot pull apart into points, and that changes the contest with the Moon.
1>4: From the single point of {prev} the night goes straight to the hardest test at {next}, light that binoculars cannot gather into points.
{prev} packed all its light into one point; {next} spreads its light into a glow, and a glow has to beat the moonlit sky on every patch at once.

At {next} two or more points share the field, and the moonlit sky falls on each of them alike.
With {next} the question becomes whether the Moon can take one star of a group and leave its neighbor, and brightness alone decides.

At {next} a whole crowd of stars meets the moonlit sky, and the Moon's cut runs right through it.
{next} holds stars of many brightnesses at once, the ideal place to see exactly where moonlight draws its line.

{next} spreads its light the thinnest of anything tonight, so it is the place to see how far into the glow the Moon lets you go.
At {next} the light no longer comes in points at all, and a glow has to beat the moonlit sky on every patch at once.

AST-Coathanger.beat: A crowd that is not a family
AST-Coathanger.question: Does the Moon treat the Coathanger, a chance pattern, any differently from a true cluster?
AST-Coathanger.why: The Coathanger looks like a cluster but is a chance line-up of unrelated stars, which makes it a neat test of what moonlight cares about.
AST-Coathanger.look: Sweep a little less than halfway from Albireo toward Altair, into Vulpecula: a bar of six stars with a hook of four below its middle. A couple of the hook stars look orange; the whole pattern is easy tonight.
AST-Coathanger.answer: The Moon responds only to how bright each point looks, not to whether the stars belong together. Most of the Coathanger's stars are bright enough, so the pattern survives, its faintest members a little weaker.
AST-Coathanger.story: Whether a pattern survives moonlight depends on its faintest essential star, the one without which the shape falls apart. The Coathanger's bar and hook are drawn by stars of several brightnesses, and the faintest go first, while a true cluster would lose members in exactly the same order. The Moon sorts by brightness alone; telling family from strangers needs measured distances and motions.

AST-Hyades.question: Why do the Hyades survive moonlight better than most star clusters?
AST-Hyades.why: The Hyades are the nearest open cluster, a V of stars wide enough to need several binocular fields, and their nearness matters a great deal tonight.
AST-Hyades.look: Sweep along each arm of the V of Taurus. Dozens of white and yellow stars and a few orange giants are still there, while faint background stars have thinned; Aldebaran at one tip is a foreground star.
AST-Hyades.answer: Being so close, the Hyades’ members look bright, and bright points stand well above the moonlit sky. A more distant family of the same stars would look fainter and lose many more members to the glow.
AST-Hyades.story: Over hundreds of millions of years the heavier stars of a cluster sink toward its middle while lighter ones drift outward, much as heavier objects settle in a shaken jar. In the Hyades this sorting is well measured, so the faint members a bright Moon removes are mostly from the cluster's outskirts. The heart of the V, drawn in its heaviest and brightest members, is exactly what survives.

AST-OrionBelt.beat: A crowd: the Belt’s family, thinned
AST-OrionBelt.question: What happens to the chain of stars winding through Orion’s Belt in moonlight?
AST-OrionBelt.why: Orion’s Belt is three bright stars set in a loose young family of fainter ones, so it shows how a group is pared down to its brightest.
AST-OrionBelt.look: Put the middle Belt star in the center and let the outer two sit near the edges. The S-shaped chain of fainter stars winding through the field is thinner tonight, while the three blue-white Belt stars are untouched.
AST-OrionBelt.answer: The faint members of the chain sink below the moonlit sky, and the three Belt stars, far brighter, stay. The family is the same; the Moon simply shows you only its brightest children.
AST-OrionBelt.story: Nature makes stars the way it makes pebbles on a beach, a few big ones and a great many small, and Edwin Salpeter put numbers to that in 1955 by counting the stars of each mass near the Sun. Few as they are, the heavyweights give out most of a young group's light, so the Moon can remove most of the Belt family's members while taking only a small share of its total glow.

Cr69.beat: A crowd: a compact bright triangle
Cr69.question: Why does the λ Orionis Cluster survive the Moon when so much of Orion fades?
Cr69.why: The λ Orionis Cluster is a neat little triangle of stars at Orion’s head, with no visible nebula to lose, so it shows what a crowd of points keeps.
Cr69.look: Aim at the faint star that marks Orion’s head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn it into a neat little triangle with fainter stars around it; the triangle is clear tonight, the faintest stars thinner.
Cr69.answer: Its main stars are bright points that stand above the moonlit sky, and the faint ring of gas around them is beyond binoculars on any night, so the Moon has no nebula here to take. Only its faintest members drop out.
Cr69.story: Your eye adds up light for only about a tenth of a second before starting afresh, while a camera can add it up for minutes. That is why photographs show a vast, faint ring of glowing gas around this cluster that binoculars never show, even on the darkest night. It is also why the Moon's glow, which the camera adds up too, spoils long exposures as surely as it spoils the view. For the eye, the cluster has only ever been its stars.

DS-16Dra.beat: Two points: a faint, easy pair
DS-16Dra.question: How faint can a pair be and still split easily under a bright Moon?
DS-16Dra.why: 16 and 17 Draconis are two modest white stars, fainter than most of tonight’s sights, which makes them a test of how far down binoculars can go in moonlight.
DS-16Dra.look: In Draco, two matched white points sit 90″ apart, an easy split for any binoculars. Tonight they look a little less sparkling than on a dark night, but both are plainly there.
DS-16Dra.answer: A pair can be quite faint, because binoculars gather far more light than your eye and keep each star a point while the moonlit sky gets no brighter in the view. These fifth-magnitude stars are hard to see by eye tonight, yet the pair is easy through the glass.
DS-16Dra.story: On a dark night the naked eye reaches stars of about the sixth magnitude, but a bright Moon pulls that limit up by a step or two, and stars as faint as these sit right where the cut falls. Binoculars push the limit back down by several magnitudes, because they multiply every star's light while the sky in the view stays as it was. You can measure the difference yourself by counting the stars around Draco's head by eye and then again through the glass.

DS-56And.beat: Two points over a fading cluster
DS-56And.question: Why does the 56 Andromedae pair survive when the cluster behind it fades?
DS-56And.why: 56 Andromedae is a pair of orange stars at the edge of the scattered cluster NGC 752, so one field holds two points and a faint crowd.
DS-56And.look: In southern Andromeda, about five degrees south of Almach, the two orange stars of 56 Andromedae split clearly in any binoculars. Around them, where NGC 752’s faint stars usually scatter, the field is much emptier tonight.
DS-56And.answer: The pair are each single points bright enough to stand above the moonlit sky, while NGC 752’s members are fainter stars that sink below it. Moonlight cuts by brightness, and a cluster of faint stars is the first to feel the cut.
DS-56And.story: The faint stars of the cluster behind this pair are not all dimmer suns; some are orange giants just like the two in front, only several times farther away. Light fades with the square of distance, so each of them arrives with a fraction of the brightness. Tonight that fraction decides everything, for the near pair stays above the Moon's cut while the distant crowd falls below it. Distance, which binoculars cannot see, turns out to be one of the Moon's strongest allies.

DS-61Cyg.question: Why do binoculars show 61 Cygni more clearly than your eye, even in moonlight?
DS-61Cyg.why: 61 Cygni is a pair of faint orange stars, too dim to enjoy by eye under the Moon, which makes it the place to see what magnification does for points of light.
DS-61Cyg.look: Find 61 Cygni about 8° south-east of Deneb. In steady 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart; at 7× brace them well. The pair stands out more clearly in the eyepiece than to the naked eye.
DS-61Cyg.answer: Magnification spreads the moonlit sky over a wider view, so it looks no brighter, while the stars stay points and gain all the light the lenses collect. The background effectively darkens around them, and the pair stands out.
DS-61Cyg.story: Double-star observers have always been fond of moonlit nights, because a split depends on the steadiness of the air and the quality of the optics, not on the darkness of the sky. Measuring pairs is classic bright-time work, done on nights astronomers cannot use for faint galaxies. What spoils a split is turbulence, which makes star images boil, and observers rate each night's seeing by how steady the stars look, whatever the Moon is doing.

DS-Albireo.question: Does Albireo keep both its gold and its blue under a bright Moon?
DS-Albireo.why: Albireo is the sky’s most famous color pair, and if moonlight could blur or wash out two close points, a gold star with a blue one beside it would show it first.
DS-Albireo.look: Albireo marks the head of the swan in Cygnus. Brace your binoculars: at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white spark 34″ away, and at 7× it is tighter but still there with care. Both colors hold against tonight’s pale sky.
DS-Albireo.answer: It keeps both, because each star is its own point of light, far brighter than the moonlit sky behind it, and the Moon adds no tint. What blurs a pair is your optics and the air, never the Moon.
DS-Albireo.story: The eye judges a color by comparing how strongly the light excites three kinds of cones, tuned to red, green and blue, and Albireo's two stars excite them in very different proportions. Part of the famous contrast is your own eye as well: set side by side, each color makes the other look stronger, an effect painters exploit. The Moon adds nothing to either star's light, so neither the colors nor that contrast change.

DS-AlpCap.question: Can you still split α Capricorni with your eyes alone in moonlight?
DS-AlpCap.why: α Capricorni is a pair keen eyes can split on a dark night, so it is a quick measure of how much the Moon takes from the naked eye and what binoculars give back.
DS-AlpCap.look: α Capricorni is the upper star of the Goat’s head in Capricornus. Try it by eye first, then raise the binoculars: two warm-colored stars about a fifth of a Moon’s width apart, an easy split.
DS-AlpCap.answer: By eye it is harder tonight, because both stars are fairly faint and the brighter sky lowers their contrast. In binoculars each becomes a stronger point against a sky no brighter than before, so the split is as clean as ever.
DS-AlpCap.story: Pairs like this have served as eyesight tests for centuries, because splitting them by eye depends on two things at once, the sharpness of your vision and the contrast of the stars against the sky. Moonlight leaves sharpness alone and takes away contrast, so a pair that sharp eyes divide on a dark night can merge into one fuzzy point by eye on a moonlit one. Yet nothing about the stars or the gap between them has changed.

DS-AlpLib.beat: Two points: a wide traveling pair
DS-AlpLib.question: Why do binoculars make Zubenelgenubi’s companion easier to see on a moonlit night?
DS-AlpLib.why: Zubenelgenubi is a bright star with a fainter partner well clear of it, a pair that shows how magnification fights a bright sky.
DS-AlpLib.look: Find Libra between Spica and Antares. Center Zubenelgenubi and look just north-west, where a fainter star stands clearly apart, easy even at 7×; the bright star is white, the companion a touch creamier.
DS-AlpLib.answer: Magnification spreads the sky’s glow over a wider view, so it looks no brighter, while each star stays a point and gains all the light the lenses collect. The faint companion, which competes with the Moon by eye, stands out once the binoculars are up.
DS-AlpLib.story: Contrast is the key: what lets you see a star is how much brighter it is than the sky right around it, and the eye judges that as a ratio. Moonlight raises the sky without touching the star, so the ratio falls for every star in the field, and it falls furthest for the faint ones, which had the smallest ratio to begin with. That is why Zubenelgenubi itself looks unchanged while its companion, by eye, grows harder.

DS-DeltaCep.beat: Two points: a pulsing star and its partner
DS-DeltaCep.question: Can you still judge a star’s brightness against its neighbors when the Moon is up?
DS-DeltaCep.why: δ Cephei is the famous pulsing star, and its steady companion is a fixed yardstick, so the pair asks whether moonlight spoils comparisons between stars.
DS-DeltaCep.look: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house-shaped figure of Cepheus, with a fainter blue-white companion 41″ beside it. Compare δ with ζ and ε Cephei nearby; the comparison works under the Moon as well as on a dark night.
DS-DeltaCep.answer: Comparisons still work, because the Moon adds the same glow behind every star in the field and leaves their own light alone, so their relative brightness is unchanged. Comparing stars side by side is one kind of observing a bright Moon cannot spoil.
DS-DeltaCep.story: Variable-star observers estimate brightness exactly this way, by comparing a star with steady neighbors of known magnitude. They carry on under a full Moon, because the sky's glow lies equally behind every star they compare. Their estimates, collected by the hundreds of thousands, have traced the rise and fall of δ Cephei and its kind for more than a century. A bright Moon makes the faintest comparison stars harder to use, but the method itself is untouched.

DS-DoubleDbl.question: Why is the Double-Double harder for the naked eye tonight but easy in binoculars?
DS-DoubleDbl.why: Sharp eyes can see the Double-Double as a stretched star on a dark night, so it is a classic test of what the eye can resolve, and the Moon makes that test harder.
DS-DoubleDbl.look: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7° to the north-east: two matched white stars sit side by side in Lyra, split easily in any binoculars. By eye under tonight’s sky, the stretched look is much harder to catch.
DS-DoubleDbl.answer: These stars are faint to the naked eye, so moonlight steals much of their contrast against the sky. Binoculars gather more of their light into each point while the sky gets no brighter, so the two stars stand clear again, two points that stay two.
DS-DoubleDbl.story: Splitting a pair by eye takes contrast as well as sharpness: two points close together blur slightly into each other, and the eye must see a dip of darker sky between them. Moonlight fills that dip with glow, so the gap that sharp eyes catch on a dark night turns into an unbroken smear. In binoculars the gap is so much wider that the dip stays deep, Moon or no Moon.

DS-MizarAlcor.beat: Two points: the old eyesight test
DS-MizarAlcor.question: Why is Alcor harder to see by eye tonight, but easy in binoculars?
DS-MizarAlcor.why: Mizar and Alcor, in the Big Dipper’s handle, were a traditional eyesight test, and a bright Moon makes that test harder, which is exactly what makes them useful here.
DS-MizarAlcor.look: Look at the middle star of the Big Dipper’s handle. By eye under tonight’s sky, little Alcor beside Mizar may take effort; in binoculars the two sit well apart and both are crisp.
DS-MizarAlcor.answer: Alcor is a modest star close to a bright one, so against a moonlit sky it loses much of its contrast to the naked eye. Binoculars collect far more of its light and keep it a point while the sky in the view gets no brighter, so the pair comes back.
DS-MizarAlcor.story: Alcor is a fourth-magnitude star beside a second-magnitude one, and Mizar's own light spreads a little around it inside the eye, so on a moonlit night the faint star has two glows to beat at once. Alcor was long called an eyesight test, though under most country skies it is plain to the naked eye; a bright Moon, especially with the pair low or in haze, can push it toward the edge. The magnification of binoculars widens the gap until Mizar's halo no longer reaches Alcor.

DS-NuDra.question: Do two equally bright stars survive moonlight equally?
DS-NuDra.why: ν Draconis is a pair of matched white stars in Draco’s head, a clean experiment in how the Moon treats two points of the same brightness.
DS-NuDra.look: Find the four-star head of Draco north-west of Vega, then its faintest star. Binoculars split it into two equal white points 62″ apart, both clearly visible against tonight’s brightened sky.
DS-NuDra.answer: Two equal stars fare equally, because the Moon adds the same glow behind each and they stand the same height above it. Whatever happens to one happens to the other, so the twins stay twins even in moonlight.
DS-NuDra.story: Moonlight cannot pull two points together, because how sharp a star image is depends on your optics and the steadiness of the air, never on the sky's brightness. Astronomers grade each night's seeing by how much the air makes star images boil and spread, and a turbulent moonless night can blur a tight pair that a calm moonlit night splits cleanly. A pair as wide as ν Draconis is safe on almost any night.

DS-ThetaTau.question: Do θ¹ and θ² Tauri keep their contrasting colors with the Moon up?
DS-ThetaTau.why: θ Tauri is a wide pair inside the Hyades, one white and one yellow-orange, a color contrast right next to the cluster’s fading faint stars.
DS-ThetaTau.look: Inside the Hyades V in Taurus, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair that binoculars split at a glance. θ² is white and θ¹ yellow-orange; a slight defocus makes the contrast stronger.
DS-ThetaTau.answer: Both keep their colors, because each is a bright point well above the moonlit sky, and the Moon adds no color of its own. The cluster's faint members around them are the ones paying for the moonlight.
DS-ThetaTau.story: Color in a star is a matter of proportion: a cool star sends relatively more red and yellow light, a hot one more blue. The eye reads that balance through its three kinds of cones, as long as each gets enough light to respond. Both stars of θ Tauri are comfortably above that level, so the balance reads as clearly as on a dark night. Astronomers built their first color thermometers on the same principle, measuring each star through a blue filter and a yellow one.

HR1387.question: Which of κ Tauri’s two stars does the Moon dim more, and why?
HR1387.why: κ Tauri is an unequal pair just north of the Hyades, a bright white star with a fainter one, and the gap in brightness shows where moonlight bites.
HR1387.look: Look about 6° north of the Hyades V in Taurus. Binoculars split it into two white stars about 5.7 arcminutes apart, the fainter clearly less vivid against tonight’s sky.
HR1387.answer: Neither star gets dimmer; the sky gets brighter behind both. The fainter star simply had less to spare, so it stands closer to the glow and looks weaker, while the brighter one barely notices.
HR1387.story: Each step on the magnitude scale is a fixed ratio of brightness, about two and a half times, so a star one magnitude fainter than its partner sends well under half as much light. On a moonlit night that ratio becomes the whole story, because the sky has risen toward the fainter star's level while staying far below the brighter one's. The two stars have not changed relative to each other at all; only the floor beneath them has risen.

HR1479.question: Why does σ Tauri split as easily tonight as on a moonless night?
HR1479.why: σ Tauri is a pair of nearly equal white stars beside Aldebaran, wide enough that only moonlight, not optics, could make it hard.
HR1479.look: Look about 1° south-east of Aldebaran in Taurus. Binoculars split it into two white stars about 7.4 arcminutes apart (an arcminute is a sixtieth of a degree), nearly equal in brightness and both clear tonight.
HR1479.answer: A bright sky cannot pull two points together; it can only lower their contrast, and these stars are bright enough to keep plenty. The split depends on the gap and your optics, and the gap here is wide.
HR1479.story: Even a perfect lens turns a star into a tiny disk with faint rings, because light is a wave, and the wider the lens, the smaller the disk. Two stars split cleanly when their disks do not overlap, a matter of optics and geometry that the brightness of the sky never enters. A pair as wide as σ Tauri would split in lenses far narrower than your binoculars, and even the naked eye can manage it.

HR168.beat: A point of color: orange giant
HR168.question: Does the Moon change the colors in Cassiopeia’s W, or only the sky around them?
HR168.why: Schedar is the one orange star in Cassiopeia’s white W, a contrast that makes a quick test of what moonlight can and cannot touch.
HR168.look: Schedar is the bright southern point of Cassiopeia’s W. Swing to γ Cassiopeiae at the center of the W and back: orange against white, as clear as on a dark night, while the Milky Way’s faint glow through the W has thinned.
HR168.answer: The Moon only adds glow to the sky, the same amount behind both stars, so it cannot make Schedar less orange or γ Cassiopeiae less white. What it does take is the soft background of the Milky Way, which spreads its light too thinly to compete.
HR168.story: The Milky Way's glow is starlight too, the blended light of stars too faint and too crowded to see one by one, as Galileo found when his first telescope broke the haze into stars. Spread together, those stars make a glow only a little brighter than the dark sky itself. Raise the sky's brightness and that small margin is gone, while a single bright star like Schedar keeps an enormous one.

HR1713.beat: A point of color: blue-white supergiant
HR1713.question: How can your eye still see Rigel’s icy blue while moonlight washes the sky?
HR1713.why: Color is the first thing a dim sky steals from your eyes, so brilliant Rigel is a fair test of whether the Moon can steal it from a star.
HR1713.look: Rigel is Orion’s foot, diagonally across from Betelgeuse. Its blue-white tint is plain even against tonight’s pale sky, and a quick swing to orange Betelgeuse puts the two colors side by side.
HR1713.answer: Only the cones of your eye, its less sensitive light cells, can see color, and a faint glow never wakes them. Rigel pours so much light into one point that they fire at once, so its color survives any moonlit sky.
HR1713.story: A star's image is not a perfect point: the air smears it into a tiny shimmering disk a few arcseconds across, and your binoculars and eye spread it a little more. Even so, that disk covers so little sky that the moonlight falling on the same spot is almost nothing, while Rigel's whole output lands right there. That imbalance between a star's light and the sky behind it is why the Moon can never wash out a bright star's color.

HR2326.beat: A point of color: white supergiant
HR2326.question: Why does the moonlit sky look gray behind Canopus when it is really blue?
HR2326.why: Canopus is the second-brightest star of the night, white and steady, and it is the place to notice that the sky around it has a color your eyes cannot see.
HR2326.look: Canopus is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. High in the sky it is a steady white point in binoculars; low down it flickers through colors as our air splits its light. The sky around it looks pale gray.
HR2326.answer: Moonlight is sunlight reflected, and the air scatters it just as it does by day, so the moonlit sky is genuinely blue. It is simply too faint for the cones that see color, while Canopus pours enough light into one point to show you its true tint.
HR2326.story: The glow that moonlight spreads across the sky is made by our air, which scatters a little of the Moon's light toward you from every direction. On the Moon itself there is no air to scatter anything, so the sky stays black even at noon and bright stars would shine right beside the sunlit ground. On Earth, the higher you stand and the cleaner the air, the less light is scattered, which is why mountain observatories suffer least from a bright Moon.

HR2990.beat: A point of color: orange giant
HR2990.question: Does moonlight change the colors of Castor and Pollux, or only the sky behind them?
HR2990.why: Gemini’s twins differ in color, which makes them a ready-made test of whether a bright Moon alters the stars themselves or only the dark between them.
HR2990.look: Pollux and Castor, the two heads of Gemini, fit together in the field of most binoculars. Pollux is the brighter and orange, Castor white; defocus slightly and the difference is as clear as on any dark night.
HR2990.answer: Moonlight changes only the sky: it adds the same faint glow behind both stars, so the difference between them, a cooler orange giant beside a hotter white star, reaches you unchanged.
HR2990.story: How faint a thing can the eye see against a lit background? During the Second World War the vision scientist Richard Blackwell had observers make hundreds of thousands of judgments of faint spots on backgrounds of every brightness. What the eye detects, he found, is contrast, a spot's light compared with the light around it. Brighten the background and a faint spot needs proportionally more light to be noticed, while stars as bright as Gemini's twins have contrast to spare.

HR3165.beat: A point of color: hottest star
HR3165.question: Why does one of the hottest stars you can see look merely blue-white?
HR3165.why: Naos is about as hot as a naked-eye star gets, and its color, which survives the Moon untouched, is a lesson in what the eye can and cannot read.
HR3165.look: In binoculars Naos is a sharp, steely blue-white point in Puppis, clear against the moonlit sky. Swing about 10° west to Pi Puppis, a deep yellow-orange star, for the other end of the color range.
HR3165.answer: Beyond a certain heat, extra temperature barely changes a star’s visible color, because most of the added light is ultraviolet your eyes cannot see. So Naos looks only a little bluer than cooler blue-white stars, and the Moon, which adds no color of its own, leaves that tint as it is.
HR3165.story: Moonlight does not spread evenly: the sky is brightest close to the Moon, where haze scatters its light forward, and darkest about a right angle away from it. Astronomers measured this on Mauna Kea and turned it into a formula that observatories still use to predict how bright each patch of a moonlit sky will be. A star's color survives anywhere, but on a moonlit night faint things are best hunted well away from the Moon.

HR3207.beat: Two points: a bright star and its retinue
HR3207.question: Which members of the little Gamma Velorum group can the Moon take away?
HR3207.why: Gamma Velorum is a bright star with companions of very different brightness, a small ladder for measuring where moonlight starts to win.
HR3207.look: Steady your binoculars and Gamma Velorum splits into a bright white star with a fainter one 41″ beside it. Two much fainter stars farther out complete the group on a dark night; tonight expect to miss at least the fainter of them.
HR3207.answer: The faintest go first, because they stand only slightly above a dark sky and sink once the Moon brightens it. The bright star and its fourth-magnitude companion stay, each a point far above the glow.
HR3207.story: The stars of Gamma Velorum's group make a ladder of brightness, from second magnitude down toward the edge of binocular sight, and moonlight saws off the bottom rungs. Where the cut falls depends on more than the Moon's phase: its height in the sky, the haze in the air and how high Vela stands all move it. The same group can lose one member on one moonlit night and two on another.

HR3307.beat: A point of color: blended pair
HR3307.question: Can a color made by blending two stars survive moonlight as well as a pure one?
HR3307.why: Avior is the orange corner of the False Cross, and its color is a blend of two stars too close to split, a subtle mixture to test against the Moon.
HR3307.look: Avior is the brightest star of the False Cross and the only one with a clear orange tint. Compare it with white Delta Velorum and Aspidiske, the other corners.
HR3307.answer: A blended color survives just as well, because the two stars’ light arrives mixed into one point, and the Moon only adds glow behind it. The cool orange giant outshines its hot blue companion, and the moonlit sky cannot change that balance.
HR3307.story: Moonlight is sunlight, and the air scatters its blue far more than its red, so a moonlit sky is brightest in the blue and much darker in the red and infrared. Observatories make use of this: on nights near full Moon they turn to red and infrared work, where the glare matters least. An orange star like Avior puts most of its light where the moonlit sky is darkest, which helps its warm color come through.

HR337.beat: A point of color: red giant
HR337.question: Why does Mirach shine on while the galaxy beside it nearly disappears?
HR337.why: Mirach, the ruddy middle star of Andromeda, is the usual signpost to the Andromeda Galaxy, so one short sweep spans the easiest and hardest things for a moonlit sky.
HR337.look: Mirach is the middle bright star of Andromeda’s chain, a ruddy orange point in binoculars, untroubled by the Moon. Hop north-west through μ Andromedae toward the Andromeda Galaxy and see how little of its glow is left.
HR337.answer: Mirach’s light arrives in a single point, while the galaxy spreads its light over a patch of sky several times wider than the full Moon. Moonlight adds the same glow to every patch, so the point wins and the galaxy, bright in total but thin on any one patch, mostly loses.
HR337.story: Astronomers measure this contest with a unit made for it, the magnitude per square arcsecond, the brightness of a patch of sky an arcsecond on a side. A dark country sky and the faint outer disk of a galaxy both score dim values on that scale, while a star, whose light lands in one tiny image, scores almost unimaginably bright. Moonlight raises the sky's score, and anything that does not beat the new value patch for patch disappears.

HR3634.beat: A point of color: orange supergiant
HR3634.question: Why does Suhail look more colorful through binoculars than to your eye?
HR3634.why: Suhail, the bright orange star of Vela, shows what binoculars add to color on a night when the sky is fighting your eyes.
HR3634.look: Suhail is the bright orange star about 11° east-north-east of Gamma Velorum. Through binoculars its orange is clear; defocus a little to make it glow, then swing to blue-white Gamma Velorum.
HR3634.answer: Binoculars collect far more of Suhail’s light and still deliver it to one point, while the moonlit sky, spread out by the magnification, looks no brighter than before. More light on the same spot pushes the star further past the threshold for color.
HR3634.story: Your eyes adapt to darkness in two stages, a quick one by the cones and a slow one by the rods, which rebuild their light-sensitive pigment over the better part of half an hour. A bright Moon never lets the rods finish, and a single glance at it undoes much of their progress, so on moonlit nights it pays to keep the Moon out of your view. Color vision does not wait for that slow adaptation, which is why Suhail's orange is ready the moment you look.

HR3982.beat: A point of color: blue-white star
HR3982.question: If the Moon leaves Regulus alone, why can its faint companion vanish tonight?
HR3982.why: Regulus, the bright heart of Leo, comes with a small companion that is easy on a dark night, which makes the pair a first glimpse of where moonlight begins to bite.
HR3982.look: Regulus is the bright star at the bottom of Leo’s backward question mark, crisp and blue-white in binoculars. Brace them and look a short way to the north-west for faint Regulus B; tonight it may be very hard or simply gone.
HR3982.answer: The Moon adds the same glow behind both stars, and Regulus stands far above it while its eighth-magnitude companion barely rose above a dark sky to begin with. Brightness, not closeness, decides who survives, a rule the rest of the night keeps confirming.
HR3982.story: A faint star beside a brilliant one fights two glows at once: the moonlit sky, and the bright star's own halo of light scattered inside your binoculars and your eye. Each adds to the background the companion has to beat, and together they can push it below what the eye can pick out. On a dark night the halo is its only enemy, which is why the companion that may vanish tonight is an easy catch under a moonless sky.

HR4301.beat: A point of color: yellow-orange giant
HR4301.question: Why does the Big Dipper look complete when the Moon has hidden so much else?
HR4301.why: The Big Dipper is the most familiar pattern in the northern sky, and Dubhe, its yellow-orange pointer star, shows why the Moon leaves such patterns whole.
HR4301.look: Dubhe is the upper pointer of the Dipper’s bowl, with Merak five degrees below it. Sweep between them a few times: Dubhe is yellow-orange and Merak white, both crisp, while the faint stars around the bowl are thinner than usual.
HR4301.answer: The Dipper is drawn entirely in bright stars, and moonlight removes only the faint ones. Dubhe and its partners each pack their light into a point far brighter than the glow behind it, so the outline you know stays exactly as it is.
