STAR-Capella.story: Low in the sky a bright star like Capella flashes red and green and blue, because turbulent air bends its colors along slightly different paths and they reach your eye in separate flickers. That is the air at work, not the Moon, and it calms as the star climbs. A pale tint like Capella's is best judged when the star stands high and steady, and on a moonlit night that steadiness matters more than the darkness.

STAR-Rasalgethi.beat: A point of color: red giant
STAR-Rasalgethi.question: How faint can a star be and still keep its color under the Moon?
STAR-Rasalgethi.why: Rasalgethi is much fainter than the night’s brilliant stars, yet deeply orange-red, so it probes the edge of color in a moonlit sky.
STAR-Rasalgethi.look: Rasalgethi and Rasalhague, the heads of Hercules and Ophiuchus, sit about 5° apart and fit in one low-power sweep. In binoculars Rasalgethi is orange-red and Rasalhague white; by eye alone, under tonight’s sky, the difference is much harder to see.
STAR-Rasalgethi.answer: Faint stars lose their color first because the cones of your eye need bright light, and moonlight does not help. Binoculars gather enough of Rasalgethi’s light to keep its orange-red alive, a reminder that the star never changed, only how much of it reaches your eye.
STAR-Rasalgethi.story: Rasalgethi and Rasalhague make a fair comparison because they stand so close together: the same air, the same patch of moonlit glow and the same eye judge both, so any difference you see belongs to the stars. Astronomers rely on the same trick, called differential measurement, comparing a target with a nearby reference star so that the sky and the atmosphere cancel out.

STAR-Sirius.beat: A point of color: the brightest star
STAR-Sirius.question: The Moon is vastly brighter than Sirius, so why can’t it hide it?
STAR-Sirius.why: Sirius is the brightest star of the night, and pitting it against the far brighter Moon shows where moonlight’s power actually goes.
STAR-Sirius.look: Follow Orion’s Belt down and to the left to Sirius, the blazing white star of Canis Major. Even with the Moon up it dazzles in binoculars, and low in the sky it still flashes colors as our air bends its light.
STAR-Sirius.answer: The moonlight that hides stars is the small share scattered by the air, spread over the entire sky, so the patch around Sirius gets only a sliver. Sirius puts all its light into one point, and in that tiny contest the star wins.
STAR-Sirius.story: The daytime sky is the extreme case of a moonlit one, with the Sun's scattered light bright enough to hide every star, yet astronomers have long found Sirius in full daylight with a telescope aimed at the right spot. Magnification darkens the patch of sky around a star while the star stays a point, so even the blue noon sky can be beaten. Your binoculars play the same trick tonight on a far fainter glow.

STAR-Vega.beat: A point of color: blue-white star
STAR-Vega.question: Where did Vega’s ring of faint stars go?
STAR-Vega.why: Vega, the first star to appear overhead on summer evenings, is usually surrounded in binoculars by a scatter of faint stars, and tonight’s sky shows how many of them depend on darkness.
STAR-Vega.look: Vega is the brilliant blue-white star of little Lyra. In binoculars it is a hard white spark, but count the faint stars around it: fewer than on a dark night, while the Double-Double and Lyra’s parallelogram nearby still show.
STAR-Vega.answer: They are still there, only buried: moonlight raised the sky’s glow above the faintest of them, while Vega and Lyra’s brighter stars stand far above it. What vanished were the stars that needed a dark sky; what remains is everything bright enough to ignore it.
STAR-Vega.story: Vega has a special place in how astronomers measure starlight: for decades it served as the zero point of the magnitude scale and the standard against which star colors were set. Every faint star around it is ranked by how much less light it sends, and five magnitudes is a factor of a hundred, so the faint stars that vanish tonight were already sending only a tiny fraction of Vega's light. That small margin over the dark sky is all the Moon has to erase.

lenses.storyline: A star's color is a thermometer you can read with your own eyes. Everything that glows, from a stove ring to the Sun, sends out a broad spread of colors, and the hotter it gets the more that spread tips from red toward blue. So the stops climb the scale in order: an ember-red star at the cool end, then orange, then the Sun's own yellow, then white. Blue-white comes last, at the hot end, where the eye's thermometer starts to run out of range, and when the sky allows, a pair closes the night with two temperatures in a single view. At every stop you judge the color first, against the one before it, and only then learn what it means in kelvins and why. By the end you are not being told the temperatures of the stars; you are reading them.

From {prev} to {next} the tint shifts from deep red-orange to plain orange, and that small shift is a hotter surface.
Beside the deep red of {prev}, {next} reads as a cleaner orange, the color of a surface some hundreds of degrees hotter.
1>3: From the ember of {prev}, the scale passes through orange to reach {next}, whose soft yellow belongs to a surface close to the Sun's own.
After the deep red of {prev}, {next} looks almost golden: the color has climbed through orange to a surface well over a thousand degrees hotter, close to the Sun's own.
{next} has left the red of {prev} far behind, past orange, and its soft yellow is the color of a surface close to the Sun's own temperature.

Swing from the orange of {prev} to {next} and the color pales toward yellow, the tint of a surface near the Sun's temperature.

From the orange of {prev} the reading jumps to the blue-white of {next}, where the eye's thermometer nears the top of its range.

Next to the soft yellow of {prev}, {next} reads paler still, the first mark above the Sun on the scale.
{next} keeps little of the warmth of {prev}, and whatever cream is left in its white belongs to a surface well above the Sun's temperature.
3>5: From the yellow of {prev} the scale climbs past white to {next}, a blue-white star at the hot end.
After the yellow of {prev}, {next} has a steely blue-white cast, the color of a surface several times hotter than the Sun's.

From {prev} to {next} the tint barely changes, a hint of blue at most, while the temperature leaps by thousands of degrees, which is how the top of the scale behaves.
Compare {next} with {prev}: if a faint blue edge seems to creep in, it is real, and behind that small change hides a surface thousands of degrees hotter.

{prev} gave you one white mark on the scale, and {next} now holds two different marks in the same field.

{next} is the reddest point in its part of the sky, and on the thermometer red is the cool end.

On the thermometer {next} sits at orange, below the Sun's yellow and above the ember red of the coolest stars.

{next} brings the scale to the Sun's own color, a gentle yellow that marks a surface near 6,000 K.

On the scale {next} reads white, the first mark above the Sun's own yellow.

DS-Albireo.question: Can you read two temperatures at once in Albireo's gold and blue?
DS-Albireo.why: Albireo puts two marks of the thermometer into a single binocular view, a final test of everything your eyes have learned tonight.
DS-Albireo.look: Albireo marks the head of the swan, at the foot of the Northern Cross. Brace your binoculars and at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white spark beside it, 34″ away; if the split is hard, let the image drift and watch the blue point trail behind.
DS-Albireo.answer: Your eye has just done what the spectra do, ranking the two by heat at a glance, and the gold one is cooler by some 8,600 degrees. Seen together under the same sky and through the same air, the difference can only be temperature.
DS-Albireo.story: Spectra read each of Albireo's stars separately and confirm what the eye sees: lines of metals and the first faint molecular bands in the gold giant's light, hydrogen and helium in the blue star's. That blue star spins so fast it has flung a disk of gas around its waist. Two temperatures leave two different kinds of fingerprint, and the eye catches the same difference as gold against blue.

DS-AlmaakDS.question: What temperature lies behind Almach's golden-orange glow?
DS-AlmaakDS.why: Andromeda's chain ends in a golden star, a step warmer in color than the ruddy one at its middle.
DS-AlmaakDS.look: Almach marks the eastern end of Andromeda's chain of bright stars, a golden-orange point in binoculars. Its blue companion is too close to split, so judge the gold against Mirach, the ruddier star in the middle of the chain.
DS-AlmaakDS.answer: Almach's giant runs at about 4,250 K, a few hundred degrees warmer than Mirach, which is enough to turn ruddy into golden. A telescope would show its blue companion at the other end of the scale, but binoculars keep the pair merged and the giant's color wins.
DS-AlmaakDS.story: Why does the giant's color win? Light simply adds, so an unresolved pair reads as the blend of its members weighted by how bright each one is, and here the golden giant gives out far more visible light than its companion. Through a telescope that splits the pair, the companion looks strikingly blue, partly because the eye exaggerates a color contrast when two stars sit side by side.

DS-AlpCVn.question: How hot is Cor Caroli, the blue-white star below the Dipper's handle?
DS-AlpCVn.why: A short sweep from La Superba, one of the reddest stars in the sky, shines a crisp blue-white star that closes the scale.
DS-AlpCVn.look: Cor Caroli is the brightest star below the Big Dipper's handle, a crisp blue-white in binoculars. About 7° to the north, toward Megrez, La Superba glows red-orange for contrast.
DS-AlpCVn.answer: Cor Caroli's surface is about 12,000 K, roughly twice the Sun's temperature and more than four times La Superba's, which is why the two look like ice and ember in neighboring fields.
DS-AlpCVn.story: Why does a star this hot look only blue-white and not deep blue? Its glow peaks far into the ultraviolet, and the narrow window the eye can see catches only the long tail of that glow, which slopes gently toward blue whatever the exact temperature. So the eye tells Cor Caroli from La Superba at a glance, but it would struggle to tell it from a star twice as hot.

DS-AlpLib.question: What temperature does the white of Libra's brightest star stand for?
DS-AlpLib.why: Libra's brightest star is white, with a creamier companion that binoculars split easily.
DS-AlpLib.look: Find Libra between Spica and Antares. Center Zubenelgenubi and look just north-west for its fainter companion, easy even at 7×: the bright star is white, the companion a touch creamier.
DS-AlpLib.answer: The bright star's surface is about 8,100 K, some 2,300 degrees hotter than the Sun, and its companion's creamier tint hints at a slightly cooler surface. Two stars that travel together still each carry their own temperature.
DS-AlpLib.story: A wide pair that travels together is a gift for the color thermometer, because both stars sit at the same distance behind the same dust, so any difference in tint is theirs alone. Here the brighter star is also the hotter, the usual rule for two stars in their steady middle years: the heavier one burns hotter and shines brighter at once.

DS-DeltaCep.question: How close to the Sun's own temperature is δ Cephei's yellow?
DS-DeltaCep.why: The yellow mark in Cepheus is an unusual one, because its temperature does not stay put.
DS-DeltaCep.look: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house-shaped figure of Cepheus, a yellowish point with a fainter blue-white companion close beside it. Compare its tint with the Garnet Star, a deep orange-red, about 6° to the west.
DS-DeltaCep.answer: Its surface averages close to the Sun's, swinging between about 5,400 and 6,500 K every 5.37 days, a shift too small for the eye, so the yellow you see is very nearly the Sun's own color.
DS-DeltaCep.story: A light meter fitted with blue and yellow filters catches what the eye misses: through each cycle δ Cephei's color index swings by a few tenths of a magnitude, reddest when the star is dimmest. Color and brightness move together because both are the surface heating and cooling, and that link helped show that a Cepheid's pulse is a real breathing of the star, not a companion passing in front.

DS-ThetaTau.question: Why does one star of the θ Tauri pair look white and the other yellow-orange?
DS-ThetaTau.why: θ Tauri is a naked-eye pair that holds two temperatures in one glance, and its stars are siblings, which makes the comparison especially fair.
DS-ThetaTau.look: Inside the Hyades V, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair that binoculars split at a glance. θ² is white and θ¹ yellow-orange, and a slight defocus makes the contrast stronger.
DS-ThetaTau.answer: θ² has a surface near 7,600 K, hotter than the Sun, while θ¹'s yellow-orange marks a surface cooler than the Sun's, so one small pair straddles our own star's place on the scale.
DS-ThetaTau.story: Two stars in one binocular field are the fairest color test there is, because their light passes through the same air at the same height, so the atmosphere reddens both equally. The eye also sharpens a contrast when two tints sit side by side, a trick of perception that makes θ¹ look a little more golden beside its white sibling than it would alone.

HR1017.question: Why does Mirfak look creamy-white when its siblings look blue-white?
HR1017.why: In Perseus a creamy star sits among hotter blue-white siblings, at the place where yellow fades into white.
HR1017.look: Aim at Mirfak, between Capella and Cassiopeia's W, and the field fills with blue-white stars strung in curving chains. Mirfak is a shade yellower than the rest, a creamy white that is easiest to judge with a slight defocus.
HR1017.answer: Mirfak's surface is about 6,350 K, just above the Sun's, while its siblings are much hotter, so its white carries a faint cream tint and theirs a bluish edge. Born the heaviest, it has already swollen and cooled while they have not.
HR1017.story: Siblings share a birthday and a distance, so the cluster around Mirfak is a fair test of the thermometer, with every member's light crossing the same space to reach you. Mirfak's cream against their blue-white is therefore a true difference in surface heat, and spectra confirm it, with Mirfak showing the strong metal lines of a cooler gas and its siblings the helium lines of hotter ones.

HR1084.question: Does a nearby star smaller than the Sun look warmer in color?
HR1084.why: A small, close neighbor of the Sun shows the yellow part of the scale in its own gentle way.
HR1084.look: From Zaurak, the brightest star of the river west of Rigel, move about 7° west-north-west, past δ Eridani, to the next star of similar brightness; its gentle yellow-orange tint sets it apart. Compare it with white Cursa, near Rigel, to see the next step.
HR1084.answer: Its surface is about 5,100 K, some 700 degrees cooler than the Sun's, so it glows a gentle yellow-orange. Being smaller than the Sun changes its brightness, not its color.
HR1084.story: Why is a star smaller than the Sun also cooler? A lighter star squeezes its core less, burns its fuel more gently and gives out less energy, and that smaller flow of heat leaves its surface cooler and its tint warmer. Among stars in their long, steady middle years, color is therefore a rough guide to weight as well as heat, from hot, heavy white stars down to cool, light orange ones.

HR1165.question: Why do all the bright Pleiades share the same blue-white color?
HR1165.why: The Pleiades are a family of hot young stars, and their brightest member shows the hot end of the scale.
HR1165.look: Center the Pleiades and find Alcyone, the brightest point near the middle. Every bright member shares its blue-white color; compare the whole group with orange Aldebaran, about 14° to the south-east.
HR1165.answer: Alcyone's surface is about 13,500 K, more than three times Aldebaran's, and its bright sisters are hot young stars too, all born together about 125 million years ago. A shared color here means a shared range of temperature, set by a shared youth.
HR1165.story: In long-exposure photographs the Pleiades sit in a blue haze, which is dust reflecting their light. Dust scatters blue light more readily than red, so the haze looks bluer than the stars themselves, by the same physics that makes the daytime sky blue. It is the reverse of the reddening a star suffers when seen straight through dust.

HR15.question: How hot is Alpheratz, the blue-white corner of the Great Square?
HR15.why: Along the northern side of the Great Square the colors run from ruddy Scheat to a crisp blue-white corner.
HR15.look: Alpheratz is the north-east corner of the Great Square, a crisp blue-white point in binoculars. Scheat, at the north-west corner, gives a fine orange contrast.
HR15.answer: Alpheratz's surface is about 12,900 K, three and a half times Scheat's temperature, so along one side of the Square you cross from orange-red to blue-white.
HR15.story: Astronomers read the temperature of stars like Alpheratz from a sharp step in their ultraviolet light, where hydrogen begins to absorb strongly. The size of that step changes steadily with heat, so it works as a thermometer far beyond the point where color stops helping, and for Alpheratz it confirms a surface a good deal hotter than any white star.

HR1577.question: Why does one corner of the Auriga pentagon glow orange?
HR1577.why: Auriga's pentagon holds several marks of the scale at once, and its orange corner is the warm one to start from.
HR1577.look: Look at the pentagon of Auriga, with Capella at its top: its south-western corner is ι Aurigae, distinctly orange beside yellowish Capella and white Menkalinan. Defocus slightly and the three colors line up like marks on a scale.
HR1577.answer: ι Aurigae's surface runs roughly 800 degrees cooler than Capella's, and that modest gap is enough to turn yellow into orange. Menkalinan, at about 9,000 K, is the next mark up after Capella.
HR1577.story: A century ago at Harvard, Annie Jump Cannon sorted hundreds of thousands of stars by the dark lines in their spectra, and only later did it become clear that her sequence of letters is a temperature scale. ι Aurigae falls in the class just warmer than the reddest giants, where lines of metals such as iron and calcium grow strong, and that verdict matches the orange your eye reports.

HR1605.question: What temperature does ε Aurigae's plain white stand for?
HR1605.why: Above Capella's yellow the scale turns white, and the brightest of the Kids shows the change.
HR1605.look: From Capella, drop a few degrees south to the thin triangle of the Kids; ε Aurigae is the brightest of the three. It is a steady white point, and when you swing back to Capella its yellow looks warmer by comparison.
HR1605.answer: Its surface runs at about 7,300 K, some 1,500 degrees hotter than the Sun's, and at that heat the glow's balance has moved far enough toward blue that the eye calls it white. Capella, at about 5,000 K, still holds on to its yellow.
HR1605.story: When ε Aurigae's dark companion passed in front of it from 2009 to 2011, the star's light fell to less than half, yet its color barely changed. The eclipsing body is a vast disk of dust coarse enough to block every color almost equally, unlike the fine dust between the stars. That gray dimming is one more proof that a star's brightness and its color are separate stories.

HR1607.question: How can a star be red enough to be called crimson?
HR1607.why: To calibrate a thermometer you want its coolest mark, and few stars run cooler than this carbon star, which shows its crimson for only part of its long cycle.
HR1607.look: Drop south from Rigel into Lepus and look about 3½° west-north-west of μ Leporis. Near its maximum it glows a startling deep red among white stars, best judged with short glances; near its minimum it fades beyond binoculars, so treat it as a bonus when it shows.
HR1607.answer: Hind's Crimson Star runs at less than half the Sun's surface temperature, and in air that cool carbon forms molecules and soot that soak up blue light, so its glow is filtered as well as cool. Every star you meet after it will look whiter, because every one of them is hotter.
HR1607.story: When John Russell Hind came upon it in 1845 he compared it to a drop of blood on a black field. A surface this cool sends most of its energy out as infrared, which no eye can see, so the light that reaches you is only the short red tail of a glow that mostly happens out of sight. The color also changes with the star's long cycle and is deepest near its dim point, when the surface is at its coolest.

HR1648.question: Why does W Orionis glow redder than Betelgeuse, its bright neighbor in Orion?
HR1648.why: Orion's thermometer can start even lower than Betelgeuse, with a faint carbon star whose red only binoculars reveal.
HR1648.look: Look about 7° south-west of Bellatrix, Orion's western shoulder. Among the white field stars it stands out as a warm orange-red point, and a slight defocus boosts the color.
HR1648.answer: W Orionis is nearly a thousand degrees cooler than Betelgeuse and smoky with carbon besides, so its light has lost almost all its blue before it leaves the star. It sets a low mark that every other star tonight will beat.
HR1648.story: In most stars there is more oxygen than carbon, and the two lock together into carbon monoxide, leaving no spare carbon to color the light. In W Orionis repeated dredging from the helium-burning depths has tipped that count the other way, and the leftover carbon builds molecules and grains that act like a sooty filter. Temperature sets the starting color, and the soot finishes the job.

HR1666.question: How hot is Cursa, the white star beside Orion's foot?
HR1666.why: Beside Orion's foot a nearby white star sits just below blue-white Rigel on the scale.
HR1666.look: Find Rigel and look about 3° north-west for a fainter white star: Cursa. Compare the two in one field; Cursa's white is a little softer, Rigel's a little bluer.
HR1666.answer: Cursa's surface is about 8,400 K and Rigel's about 12,100 K, yet that gap of 3,700 degrees makes only a slight difference in tint. Past white, the colors change slowly even when the temperatures change a lot.
HR1666.story: Cursa's spectrum is dominated by the dark lines of hydrogen, which reach their greatest strength in white stars of about this kind. Hydrogen absorbs those colors only when its electron sits one step up from the bottom, which takes a gas hot enough to lift it there but not so hot that it tears the electron away. The strength of the lines is therefore itself a thermometer, peaking among the white stars.

HR168.question: Why is Schedar orange when the other stars of the W look white?
HR168.why: Cassiopeia's W is mostly hot white and blue-white stars, and its one warm star gives the scale its orange mark.
HR168.look: Schedar is the bright southern point of Cassiopeia's W. Swing to γ Cassiopeiae at the center of the W and back: orange against blue-white.
HR168.answer: Schedar's surface is about 4,600 K and γ Cassiopeiae's about 28,000 K, roughly six times hotter. The tint reports heat, not power, and Schedar still outshines the Sun hundreds of times over.
HR168.story: Schedar's color also tells part of its life story. A giant like this one was once a hotter, whiter star in its long middle years, and swelling spread the same heat over a much larger surface, so the skin cooled until the eye reads it orange. Among the bright stars of the W it is the one that has moved furthest along that road, and its tint marks how far it has gone.

HR1713.question: How much hotter than Betelgeuse is the blue-white foot of Orion?
HR1713.why: The hot end of Orion's thermometer sits diagonally across the figure from Betelgeuse, so the whole scale fits inside one constellation.
HR1713.look: Rigel is Orion's foot, the brilliant blue-white star diagonally across from Betelgeuse. Hold it in the field and its icy color is unmistakable, especially just after a look at the orange shoulder.
HR1713.answer: Rigel's surface is about 12,100 K, more than three times Betelgeuse's and twice the Sun's. At that heat much of its glow pours out as ultraviolet, and the visible part we catch is tilted toward blue.
HR1713.story: Rigel's spectrum shows faint lines of helium, an element so reluctant to absorb light that only a very hot gas can make it do so. Those lines alone place Rigel above the white stars, a temperature reading that does not depend on its color at all, and they grow stronger in the hotter stars of Orion's Belt.

HR1790.question: Why is Orion's western shoulder blue-white while the eastern one is orange?
HR1790.why: Orion's western shoulder mirrors Betelgeuse across the hunter, but not on the thermometer.
HR1790.look: Put Bellatrix in the field, then swing about 7° across to Betelgeuse: blue-white against orange. Betelgeuse is usually the brighter, but brightness does not set color, so the difference you read is temperature.
HR1790.answer: Bellatrix's surface is about 22,000 K, roughly six times Betelgeuse's 3,600 K, and that gap is the whole difference between blue-white and orange. The two shoulders are neighbors in the figure and almost opposite ends of the thermometer.
HR1790.story: A star as hot as Bellatrix sends most of its energy out as ultraviolet light, which no eye can see and our atmosphere blocks. Telescopes flown above the air were needed to measure that hidden output, and only once it was counted did the true power of such stars, and their temperatures, fall into place.

HR1791.question: Why does Elnath look blue-white across the pentagon from orange ι Aurigae?
HR1791.why: The Auriga pentagon closes at a blue-white star, the hot end of a small scale that also holds orange, yellow and white.
HR1791.look: Elnath completes the Auriga pentagon and also marks the tip of the Bull's northern horn. Compare its blue-white with orange ι Aurigae, about 8° across the pentagon.
HR1791.answer: Elnath's surface is about 13,600 K, more than three times ι Aurigae's, so its light is tilted toward blue. Around one small pentagon you can read four steps of the scale.
HR1791.story: Beyond white, the eye's thermometer flattens. A star this hot peaks in the ultraviolet, and the visible part of its glow is the gently sloping tail of that peak, which looks much the same blue-white whether the star is twice the Sun's temperature or five times. That is why Elnath and ι Aurigae differ so plainly, while Elnath and far hotter stars look nearly alike.

HR1829.question: Why does Nihal look yellower than Arneb, its neighbor in the Hare?
HR1829.why: The Hare holds a yellow star and a white one in the same field, and the yellow one comes first.
HR1829.look: Put Nihal and Arneb, the two brightest stars of Lepus below Orion, in the same field, about 3° apart. Arneb looks slightly brighter and whiter, Nihal yellowish.
HR1829.answer: Nihal's surface is about 5,200 K and Arneb's about 7,300 K, so a 2,000-degree difference shows as yellow beside white. That Arneb also looks brighter has nothing to do with color, for it is a far more distant and far more powerful supergiant.
HR1829.story: If Nihal is yellow, what color is the Sun? Seen from space the Sun looks white, because its glow peaks in the middle of the visible range and the eye blends that balanced spread into white. From the ground it looks yellowish because the air scatters away some of its blue. A star a little cooler than the Sun, like Nihal, tips the balance just far enough toward red for the eye to call it yellow at night.

HR1865.question: How hot is the white supergiant of Lepus?
HR1865.why: In the Hare a white supergiant stands one notch above the yellow star beside it.
HR1865.look: Find Lepus, the Hare, below Rigel and Saiph. Arneb is its brightest star, white beside yellowish Nihal about 3° away, and Rigel above shows the next color up.
HR1865.answer: Arneb's surface is about 7,300 K, roughly 2,000 degrees hotter than Nihal and 1,500 hotter than the Sun. Its great brightness comes from size and power, but its whiteness comes from heat alone.
HR1865.story: Arneb's light crosses more than two thousand light-years, yet its white arrives nearly intact, because it lies well below the dusty plane of the Milky Way, where the space between the stars is clean. Astronomers check this by comparing its color with the temperature its spectrum gives, and for Arneb the two agree within a small margin.

HR1879.question: How hot is the star at the center of Orion's head?
HR1879.why: At Orion's head, inside a young cluster, shines a star of the hottest class, a test for any thermometer.
HR1879.look: Point at Orion's head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn the faint naked-eye smudge into a compact triangle of blue-white stars with a dozen fainter ones around it.
HR1879.answer: Meissa's surface is about 35,000 K, roughly six times the Sun's temperature and ten times Betelgeuse's, yet its color is the same steely blue-white as stars a third as hot. At this end of the scale a spectrum, not the eye, reads the temperature.
HR1879.story: Meissa belongs to the hottest class of stars, recognized by lines of helium that has lost one of its two electrons, a state only extreme heat can keep up. The strength of those lines, not the color, is how astronomers know it runs hotter than even the blue-white supergiants of Orion's Belt below it.

HR188.question: Diphda and τ Ceti share a tint, so do they share a temperature?
HR188.why: Color reports temperature, and Cetus offers a test of how far that report goes, with two stars of nearly the same tint.
HR188.look: Diphda is the brightest star of Cetus, alone in a wide, dim region south of Pisces. In binoculars it is yellow-orange; compare it with τ Ceti about fifteen degrees east, which looks a touch paler.
HR188.answer: They nearly do, for Diphda's surface is about 4,850 K and τ Ceti's about 5,300 K, close enough to look alike. Yet Diphda is a giant many times the Sun's width and τ Ceti a dwarf smaller than the Sun, because color reads temperature and nothing about size.
HR188.story: The color reports only the layer that sends out the visible light. Above that skin Diphda wears a corona of thin gas heated to millions of degrees, which radiates about two thousand times as much X-ray power as the Sun's corona, though none of it reaches the eye. So the hottest gas around a star can be the gas you cannot see at all, and the tint is the temperature of the surface, not of everything the star holds.

HR1903.question: How hot is the middle star of Orion's Belt?
HR1903.why: The middle of Orion's Belt is a blue supergiant, and it shows how hot the hot end can get.
HR1903.look: Center the middle Belt star and let the other two sit near the field edges. All three are blue-white, and the curving string of fainter stars around them shares the same steely tint.
HR1903.answer: Alnilam runs at more than four times the Sun's temperature, yet it looks hardly bluer than Rigel at half that heat, because at the hot end of the scale the visible color barely changes.
HR1903.story: Alnilam's temperature comes from the balance of lines in its spectrum, because the hotter a gas, the more of each kind of atom loses electrons. The ratio of lines from atoms in different states works like a set of thermometer marks far beyond the reach of color. Meghnad Saha worked out the rule behind this in 1920, and it is how astronomers first turned spectral classes into temperatures.

HR2004.question: Why does Saiph look no bluer than Rigel, though it is twice as hot?
HR2004.why: The hot end of the scale hides a surprise, and Orion's second foot shows where the eye's thermometer starts to run out of range.
HR2004.look: Compare Saiph with Rigel at Orion's opposite foot. Both are blue-white, Rigel brighter, and nothing in the tint tells you which is hotter.
HR2004.answer: Saiph's surface is about 26,500 K, more than twice Rigel's, yet both send the eye the same blue-white tail of their glow. Past this point the eye's thermometer saturates: it can say hot, but no longer how hot.
HR2004.story: A star as hot as Saiph pours out most of its energy as ultraviolet light, invisible to the eye and stopped by our atmosphere, so its full power could only be counted once telescopes rose above the air. What reaches your eye is the faint blue-tilted edge of that output, the same edge any very hot star shows.

HR2088.question: Why does Menkalinan look whiter than Capella at the top of the pentagon?
HR2088.why: Menkalinan is the white mark of Auriga's scale, one step below blue-white Elnath.
HR2088.look: Find the Auriga pentagon, with Capella at its top; Menkalinan is the white star at its eastern corner, about 8° from Capella. Swing between them: cream-gold against white.
HR2088.answer: Menkalinan's two stars have surfaces near 9,000 K, nearly twice Capella's, and at that heat the glow loses its gold. Its eclipses dim it a little but are far too slight for the eye.
HR2088.story: Twin stars make good thermometers. When two stars of the same temperature eclipse each other, the dips come out equally deep, because the light lost depends on how brightly each square meter of the hidden surface shines. Menkalinan's dips match closely. That confirms that both stars share one temperature, so the white you see is that temperature with no blend to untangle.

HR21.question: What temperature lies behind Caph's white-yellow glow?
HR21.why: Cassiopeia's western star shows white with a trace of yellow, a mark between the W's orange and blue-white stars.
HR21.look: Caph is the western end of the W of Cassiopeia, a clean white-yellow point. Compare it with orange Schedar, about 5° away, and with blue-white γ Cas at the center of the W.
HR21.answer: Caph's surface runs at about 6,900 K, more than a thousand degrees hotter than the Sun, so its light has lost nearly all its yellow. On the W's own scale it sits between Schedar at about 4,600 K and γ Cassiopeiae at about 28,000 K.
HR21.story: Across the W, Caph also shows how a star's spectrum shifts with heat. Compared with orange Schedar, its metal lines have faded and its hydrogen lines strengthened, while in γ Cassiopeiae lines of helium appear. Three stars of one constellation thus run through the sequence astronomers use to rank temperatures.

HR2294.question: How hot is Mirzam, the blue-white star that rises before Sirius?
HR2294.why: Five degrees from Sirius rises a fainter star with a bluer cast, the hot end of the scale in Canis Major.
HR2294.look: Look about 5° west of Sirius for a blue-white star: Mirzam. Compare the two and Sirius looks dazzling, Mirzam modest, with a slightly bluer tint.
HR2294.answer: Mirzam's surface is about 25,300 K, two and a half times as hot as Sirius, which tips its tint slightly toward blue. Its modest brightness is a matter of distance, which dims a star without touching its tint.
HR2294.story: Most of Mirzam's energy leaves as ultraviolet, invisible to the eye and blocked by our air, so its full output was only counted once telescopes flew above the atmosphere. That hidden light is why a star with a modest blue-white tint can be tens of thousands of times more powerful than the Sun.

HR2326.question: Why does Canopus shine white rather than yellow like the Sun?
HR2326.why: Past the Sun the scale turns white, and the brilliant star south of Sirius shows it best when it stands high.
HR2326.look: Canopus is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. Low in the sky our air splits its light into flickering colors, while higher up it shows a steady white.
HR2326.answer: Its surface is about 7,700 K, some 1,900 degrees hotter than the Sun's, and at that heat the glow's balance has shifted far enough toward blue that the eye sees white. The flashes of red and green near the horizon belong to our atmosphere, not to the star.
HR2326.story: Astronomers measure colors against a reference: by convention a star like Vega has a color index of zero, so cooler stars come out positive and hotter ones negative. Canopus lands just on the positive side, the mark of a white star a little cooler than Vega, which is exactly the faint warmth it shows beside icier Sirius.

HR2405.question: Why does one faint star in Auriga glow orange-red among white neighbors?
HR2405.why: Auriga's brilliant stars make a fine scale, but its cool end is a faint carbon star that shows its warmth only in binoculars.
HR2405.look: Look in eastern Auriga, between Capella and the Gemini twins: among white stars, one glows orange-red. Judge its color with short glances rather than a stare, since faint red stars play tricks on a tired eye.
HR2405.answer: UU Aurigae runs at less than half the Sun's surface temperature, so it starts out red, and its carbon-laden air deepens the red further. Capella, a sweep to the west, is nearly twice as hot and glows yellow.
HR2405.story: In the 1860s Angelo Secchi, sorting stars by the patterns in their spectra, set aside a small group whose light was cut by broad dark bands, and those bands turned out to be carbon molecules. Molecules like these hold together only in a cool atmosphere, so the bands are a second thermometer, and in UU Aurigae they agree with the color that this is among the coolest surfaces a binocular star can show.

HR2553.question: Why does Tau Puppis look warmer in color than Canopus nearby?
HR2553.why: Beside the brilliant white of Canopus sits a modest giant with a warmer tint, and that contrast is the next reading.
HR2553.look: In binoculars Tau Puppis is a soft yellow-orange point. Compare it with brilliant white Canopus about 5° to the west-south-west.
HR2553.answer: Tau Puppis runs roughly 3,000 degrees cooler than Canopus, which shines at about 7,700 K, and that difference shows as yellow-orange against white.
HR2553.story: A star's color comes from the shape of its whole glow, not from any single wavelength, and that shape depends on temperature alone. Tau Puppis and Canopus differ in size, age and power, yet the eye ranks them correctly by heat the moment both are in view, because none of those other differences can bend the balance of red to blue.

HR2618.question: Why does Adhara look bluer than Sirius, though fainter?
HR2618.why: In the triangle south-east of Sirius a fainter star waits, a test of whether brightness or color is the better guide to heat.
HR2618.look: Find the triangle of bright stars south-east of Sirius; Adhara is the westernmost and brightest of them. Compare its blue-white with Sirius' whiter glare and with creamy Wezen beside it.
HR2618.answer: Adhara's surface is about 22,000 K, more than twice Sirius', so its glow leans further toward blue. It looks fainter only because of distance, and distance never changes a color.
HR2618.story: Adhara is the brightest source in the sky of extreme ultraviolet light, the hard, short-wave radiation that hot stars pour out and that the hydrogen between the stars normally swallows. Toward Adhara a tunnel of thin gas lets it through, and satellites above the air found it outshining every other star at those wavelengths, a direct glimpse of the hidden glow its blue-white tint only hints at.

HR264.question: How hot is the blue-white star at the center of Cassiopeia's W?
HR264.why: The middle star of Cassiopeia's W is the hottest of the five, with orange Schedar right beside it.
HR264.look: γ Cas is the middle star of the W, a clean blue-white point in binoculars. Swing to orange Schedar, the next bright star west, and back.
HR264.answer: γ Cassiopeiae's surface is about 28,000 K, roughly six times Schedar's temperature, yet the difference in tint is only blue-white against orange. The disk of gas it sheds changes its brightness over the decades, while the star beneath stays much the same.
HR264.story: γ Cassiopeiae is a reminder that brightness can change while color stays put. Over the past century it has brightened and faded by more than a magnitude as its disk of gas grew and dissolved. Yet observers have always seen the same blue-white, and the temperature of the star beneath, read from its helium lines, has hardly moved.

HR2693.question: How hot is the creamy-yellow star in Canis Major's triangle?
HR2693.why: Where yellow shades into white, a supergiant in Canis Major sits right on the boundary.
HR2693.look: In Canis Major's triangle south-east of Sirius, Wezen is the creamy-yellow star. Compare it with blue-white Adhara, about 3° away, for a temperature ladder in one sweep.
HR2693.answer: Its surface is about 6,200 K, a little hotter than the Sun, which is why its yellow is pale and creamy. Adhara beside it burns at about 22,000 K, and the gap shows plainly as cream against blue-white.
HR2693.story: For a star as luminous as Wezen, astronomers do not rely on color alone, because its light crosses well over a thousand light-years of space and picks up a little dust on the way. They read the temperature from the ratios of particular dark lines in its spectrum, which dust cannot change, and the result confirms that the creamy tint is very nearly the star's own.

HR2773.question: What does the deep orange of Pi Puppis say about its surface?
HR2773.why: Puppis spans the thermometer in a single short sweep, and its deep orange star is the warm mark to start from.
HR2773.look: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange, with a much fainter star just beside it, an easy binocular pair. Defocus slightly and its warmth deepens against the paler stars scattered around it.
HR2773.answer: Its surface is near 3,900 K, about two-thirds of the Sun's, so its glow leans to red and the eye calls it deep orange. Every other bright star in this sweep of Puppis runs hotter, and the scale climbs from here.
HR2773.story: Two stars of the same orange can be very different beasts, and the spectrum tells them apart. The pattern of lines sets the temperature, while their sharpness reveals the pressure in the atmosphere, low in a bloated supergiant and higher in a compact star, and by that reading Pi Puppis is a supergiant. Its glow therefore comes from a surface vastly larger than the Sun's, a cool skin spread wide enough to outshine thousands of Suns.

HR2845.question: Why does Gomeisa look bluer than Procyon right beside it?
HR2845.why: Four degrees from creamy Procyon sits a star with a bluer tint, the hot end of the scale in Canis Minor.
HR2845.look: Put Procyon and Gomeisa, in the little constellation Canis Minor, in one sweep and compare colors: Procyon is creamy white, Gomeisa bluer.
HR2845.answer: Gomeisa's surface is about 11,800 K and Procyon's about 6,600 K, so the hotter star's glow leans toward blue. Procyon only looks brighter because it is about fourteen times closer.
HR2845.story: Beyond white, the eye's thermometer flattens: a star hotter than this peaks in the ultraviolet, and the part of its glow the eye can see is a gently sloping tail that changes little as the temperature climbs. Gomeisa sits just past that bend, hot enough to look bluer than Procyon, and far hotter stars would look to you almost exactly like it.

HR2891.question: What temperature gives Castor its clean white, beside orange Pollux?
HR2891.why: Gemini's white twin, four and a half degrees from its orange brother, sits near the top of the white range.
HR2891.look: Compare Castor's white with Pollux's orange, 4½° away. At 10× Castor looks single, because its two bright stars sit only 5 arcseconds apart, and their light merges into one white point.
HR2891.answer: Castor's surface runs at about 9,550 K, nearly twice Pollux's temperature, so the twins sit far apart on the scale. Castor's six stars blend into that single reading, which its bright white pairs dominate.
HR2891.story: Castor's two bright stars sit close to the temperature at which hydrogen's dark lines are strongest. Those lines need hydrogen atoms whose electron has been lifted one step up but not torn away, and that balance is best struck in white stars like these. In cooler stars too few atoms are lifted, and in hotter ones too many are stripped bare.

HR2990.question: How can the twins of Gemini wear such different colors?
HR2990.why: Gemini's twins are a lesson in color, and the warmer twin is where this step of the scale begins.
HR2990.look: Put Pollux and Castor in one field, 4½° apart: Pollux is orange, Castor white, and a touch of defocus makes the difference vivid.
HR2990.answer: Castor runs at about 9,550 K, nearly twice Pollux's temperature, so one twin glows orange and the other white. They are twins in name only, a cool giant beside a hot white star.
HR2990.story: Why are orange giants so common among the bright stars? When a star like Pollux runs out of hydrogen in its core, its outer layers swell, and the same energy spread over a much larger surface leaves each square meter cooler, so a star that was once white settles into orange. Pollux very likely shone white in its youth, much as Castor does now, which makes the twins snapshots of a change in color that comes with age.

HR3165.question: Why doesn't Naos, at the top of the scale, look deep blue?
HR3165.why: Naos sits at the very top of the scale in Puppis, one of the hottest stars the naked eye can see, and it tests how far the eye's thermometer can reach.
HR3165.look: In binoculars Naos is a sharp, steely blue-white point among many fainter Milky Way stars. Swing about 10° west to deep yellow-orange Pi Puppis and you have both ends of the scale in neighboring fields.
HR3165.answer: Its surface is about 40,000 K, nearly seven times the Sun's, so almost all of its output comes out as ultraviolet and the visible part we catch is only a gently sloping tail. That tail looks blue-white for any star hot enough, which is why the eye's thermometer tops out here.
HR3165.story: Heat this extreme turns light into a push. Naos's ultraviolet glare is caught by atoms in its own outer layers and shoves them outward, driving a wind that streams off at more than two thousand kilometers a second. That wind carries off mass many millions of times faster than the Sun's gentle breeze and will strip away a sizable part of the star, so here a temperature also foretells a star giving itself back to space.

HR3307.question: How can a blend of two stars still read as orange?
HR3307.why: Orange marks a step up from red, but a star's color can be a blend, and Avior, the warm corner of the False Cross, hides a second star in its light.
HR3307.look: Avior is the brightest star of the False Cross and the only one with a clear orange tint. Compare it with white Aspidiske at the other southern corner of the figure, and defocus slightly to make the difference plain.
HR3307.answer: Its light blends a cool orange giant near 4,300 K with a hot blue companion, and because the giant gives out more visible light, the mixture reads orange. A blended thermometer reading reports mostly the brighter partner.
HR3307.story: Each star's share of a blend depends on which colors you look in. In yellow and red light the cool giant gives out far more, but toward the ultraviolet the hot companion takes over, since a surface as cool as the giant's sends out almost nothing at such short wavelengths. Seen by an ultraviolet camera above the air, the same pair would read as a hot star, so which partner a blend reports depends on the light you collect.

HR337.question: How cool is the ruddy star in the middle of Andromeda's chain?
HR337.why: Andromeda's chain of stars runs from ruddy to golden to blue-white, and the reading begins at its ruddy middle.
HR337.look: Mirach is the middle bright star of Andromeda's chain, a ruddy orange point in binoculars. Sweep along the chain to Alpheratz and back and the difference in warmth is plain.
HR337.answer: Mirach's surface is about 3,800 K, cooler than the Sun by some 2,000 degrees, which tips its light toward red. Almach, at the end of the chain, looks golden rather than ruddy, the sign of a surface a few hundred degrees hotter.
HR337.story: Mirach's spectrum is crossed by faint bands of titanium oxide, a molecule that falls apart in any hotter atmosphere, so finding it is a temperature reading of its own. The letters astronomers use to rank stars, running O, B, A, F, G, K, M from hot to cool, were sorted out largely from clues like this, and Mirach sits at the start of the last and coolest class.

HR3541.question: How cool is the red star hiding near the Beehive?
HR3541.why: Near the Beehive hides a star you would pass over if not for its color, and that color makes it the bottom mark of the scale.
HR3541.look: From the Beehive, the misty patch in Cancer between Regulus and the Gemini twins, move about four and a half degrees south-east. X Cancri stands out by its warm red-orange, which seems to deepen the longer you look.
HR3541.answer: X Cancri runs at less than half the Sun's surface temperature, about as cool as any star binoculars can show. Regulus, about 18° to the south-east, runs more than four times hotter, which is nearly the whole span of the scale in two stars.
HR3541.story: Faint red stars play a trick on the eye: the longer you stare, the brighter and redder they seem, because the eye's response to dim red light keeps building while it watches. Variable-star observers learned long ago to judge such stars with quick glances, and X Cancri, with its deep tint, is a good place to catch the effect at work. The color itself is the honest part, the reading of a surface far too cool to glow white.

HR3699.question: Why is Aspidiske white while Avior, across the False Cross, is orange?
HR3699.why: The False Cross has a warm corner and a white one, and this is the white.
HR3699.look: Aspidiske marks one corner of the False Cross. Compare its white with Avior's orange, about 7° away at the other southern corner of the figure.
HR3699.answer: Aspidiske's surface is about 7,100 K and Avior's cool giant about 4,300 K, so the False Cross holds a span of some 2,800 degrees between two corners. Your eye sees it as white against orange.
HR3699.story: Aspidiske is a supergiant, and supergiants are harder to place by eye alone, because their thin, extended atmospheres draw sharp spectral lines unlike those of ordinary white stars. Astronomers read its temperature from the balance of hydrogen and metal lines, and the result sits comfortably above the Sun's, as the eye's verdict of white suggests.

HR3982.question: What temperature does the blue-white heart of Leo stand for?
HR3982.why: Leo's heart glows blue-white where its mane glows golden, and the heart is the hot end.
HR3982.look: Regulus is the bright dot at the bottom of the backward question mark of Leo's head, crisp and blue-white in binoculars. Swing up the Sickle to golden Algieba and back.
HR3982.answer: Regulus runs at about 11,500 K, roughly twice the Sun's temperature and two and a half times Algieba's, so Leo's brightest star looks steely where its mane looks warm. Its fast spin leaves the equator cooler than the poles, a small spread inside one reading.
HR3982.story: On the astronomers' color index Regulus comes out slightly negative, meaning it is a little brighter in blue light than in yellow, the reverse of every cooler star in Leo. That small minus sign is all the eye's blue-white amounts to, and it shows how compressed the hot end really is: Regulus and stars several times hotter differ in color index by only a few tenths.

HR403.question: How hot is Ruchbah, the white star in Cassiopeia's W?
HR403.why: In Cassiopeia's W a white star sits between the orange of Schedar and the blue-white of γ Cassiopeiae.
HR403.look: Ruchbah is the fourth star of the W, counting from Caph. It looks white, much like γ Cas next door; defocus both and γ shows a slightly bluer edge.
HR403.answer: Ruchbah runs at about 7,800 K, some 2,000 degrees hotter than the Sun, against roughly 28,000 K for γ Cassiopeiae. Though γ is more than three times hotter, the two whites differ only slightly, because the eye's color scale flattens at the hot end.
HR403.story: Why does the eye flatten the hot end? Color vision works by comparing how strongly three kinds of cone cells respond. Once a star's glow peaks beyond violet, the visible part keeps nearly the same balance among the three, even as the star's total output soars into the ultraviolet. Ruchbah and γ Cassiopeiae differ enormously in heat but only slightly in that balance.

HR4057.question: Why does Algieba shine golden in the mane of Leo?
HR4057.why: Leo's mane glows golden while its heart glows blue-white, and the golden star is the warmer mark to read first.
HR4057.look: Algieba is the brightest star of Leo's Sickle after Regulus. Binoculars cannot split its two golden giants, so judge the merged point: a warm orange-gold, plainly warmer than Regulus at the Sickle's foot.
HR4057.answer: Together they read orange-gold, the color of surfaces about 1,300 degrees cooler than the Sun's. Regulus at the foot of the Sickle runs about two and a half times hotter and glows blue-white for the opposite reason.
HR4057.story: Algieba's two giants differ slightly in tint, the brighter a shade more orange and the fainter a shade more golden, but only a telescope shows them apart. Binoculars hand you their blended light, which is how most stars reach us, as an unresolved sum. Astronomers untangle such sums with spectra, where each star's lines shift back and forth with its orbit and can be assigned to the right partner.

HR4199.question: How hot is the brightest star of the Southern Pleiades?
HR4199.why: The Southern Pleiades are led by a hot blue-white star at the top of the scale in Carina.
HR4199.look: Theta Carinae is the brightest of a loose group of blue-white stars visible even to the naked eye. In binoculars the group spans about a degree, a compact spray in the middle of the field, all sharing its bluish tint.
HR4199.answer: Its surface runs at about 31,000 K, more than five times the Sun's temperature. Even so its color is the same blue-white as stars a third as hot, because the eye cannot read heat this extreme.
HR4199.story: A star this hot pours most of its light out as ultraviolet, and its spectrum shows lines of helium strong enough to place it among the hottest stars of Carina. The eye, which sees only the visible tail of that glow, calls it simply blue-white, so the full measure of its heat comes from the spectrum and from satellites above the air.

HR424.question: What temperature does the North Star's pale yellow stand for?
HR424.why: The North Star is also a mark on the thermometer, a supergiant whose tint sits at the Sun's end of the scale.
HR424.look: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper's bowl up to Polaris. Binoculars show it on a little loop of fainter stars, the Engagement Ring; its pale yellow is subtle, so compare it with orange Kochab, about 16 degrees away.
HR424.answer: Polaris runs at about 6,000 K, a couple of hundred degrees hotter than the Sun, which makes its light a creamy yellow-white. Kochab, at about 4,100 K, shows what nearly 2,000 degrees less looks like.
HR424.story: Polaris pulses, swelling and shrinking slightly every few days, yet its tint never visibly changes, because its temperature swings by only a few tens of degrees, far below anything the eye can detect. Astronomers follow that small swing through the changing strengths of lines in its spectrum, a thermometer far finer than color.

HR4301.question: Why is Dubhe yellow-orange when Merak, the other pointer, is white?
HR4301.why: The Big Dipper is a thermometer hiding in plain sight, and its upper pointer star holds the warm end.
HR4301.look: Dubhe is the upper pointer star of the Big Dipper's bowl, and Merak, the lower one, is five degrees away. In binoculars Dubhe is yellow-orange and Merak white, so sweep between them a few times.
HR4301.answer: Dubhe's surface is about 4,700 K and Merak's about 9,500 K, so the two pointers differ by a factor of two in temperature. At the far end of the handle, blue-white Alkaid is hotter still.
HR4301.story: Dubhe and Merak make a clean demonstration that color has nothing to do with brightness, since the two pointers look much alike in brightness and their tints still disagree. Astronomers put numbers on the difference with the color index, a star's brightness through a blue filter minus its brightness through a yellow one. Dubhe's comes out large, while Merak's sits near zero, the mark of a star much like Vega.

HR4357.question: What does Zosma's white say about the heat of its surface?
HR4357.why: On the lion's back a white star sits between golden Algieba and blue-white Regulus, the next mark up.
HR4357.look: Zosma and its neighbor Chertan form the lion's back in Leo, with Denebola at the tail. In binoculars Zosma is white; compare it with golden Algieba in the mane.
HR4357.answer: Zosma runs some 2,400 degrees hotter than the Sun and nearly twice as hot as Algieba, so the gold of the mane gives way to white on the back. Regulus, hotter again, adds a blue edge.
HR4357.story: A surface as hot as Zosma's sends the peak of its glow into the ultraviolet, beyond violet, so even the visible light you see is tilted slightly toward blue. The Sun's peak sits in the middle of the visible range, which the eye reads as neutral, and between the two peaks lies the whole step from the gold of the lion's mane to the white of its back.

HR4630.question: Why does Corvus, the crow, have one orange star among its whiter ones?
HR4630.why: The little crow of Corvus holds three marks of the thermometer within a couple of binocular fields, and its orange star comes first.
HR4630.look: Corvus is the small four-star kite south-west of Spica. Minkar is the most orange of its stars; compare it with pale yellow Kraz and blue-white Gienah, each about five degrees away.
HR4630.answer: Kraz runs at about 5,100 K and Gienah at about 12,400 K, so in one small kite the colors climb from Minkar's orange through yellow to blue-white.
HR4630.story: Corvus is a fair test bench, because its tints come from stars at quite different distances and the colors still rank them correctly. Distance dims a star without changing its tint, so the order of colors you see is the order of temperatures, whichever crow star happens to lie nearest.

HR4662.question: Why does Gienah look blue-white when its crow-mates are orange and yellow?
HR4662.why: The little crow's thermometer finishes with a crisp blue-white star.
HR4662.look: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Gienah is crisply blue-white; swing to orange Minkar or pale yellow Kraz to compare.
HR4662.answer: Gienah runs at roughly twice the Sun's temperature and nearly three times Minkar's, so its glow tips toward blue. Within one small kite of stars you have read three marks of the scale.
HR4662.story: Among stars still burning hydrogen in their cores, surface heat follows weight, and Gienah's blue-white goes with a star of about four Suns. Such a star shines some three hundred times as brightly as the Sun and spends its fuel to match, so Gienah is only about 160 million years old, born while dinosaurs walked the Earth. Read this way, a tint is a rough scale and a clock as well as a thermometer.

HR472.question: What temperature lies behind Achernar's icy blue-white?
HR472.why: At the end of the long river of Eridanus a lone brilliant star closes the scale.
HR472.look: Look for the lone brilliant blue-white star at the end of the long, faint river of Eridanus. Binoculars show a sharp point; compare its icy color with creamy Alpha Hydri about 5° away.
HR472.answer: Achernar's surface is about 14,800 K, roughly two and a half times the Sun's temperature, so its glow tips firmly toward blue, the hot end of the scale in this part of the sky.
HR472.story: Achernar spins so fast that it is flattened, and a flattened star is hotter at its poles than at its stretched-out waist, by many thousands of degrees in its case. The blue-white you see is an average over that patchwork, weighted by how the star happens to be tilted toward us.

HR4730.question: How hot is Acrux, the blue-white foot of the Southern Cross?
HR4730.why: The foot of the Southern Cross is the hot end of a figure whose top star glows orange.
HR4730.look: Acrux is the bright star at the bottom of the Cross, blue-white in binoculars with a much fainter star beside it. Swing about 6° up to orange Gacrux at the top and back.
HR4730.answer: Acrux's surface is about 21,000 K, nearly six times Gacrux's temperature, so the Cross runs from orange-red at the top to blue-white at the foot. Both bright stars hidden inside Acrux are hot, so their blend keeps the same steely tint.
HR4730.story: Photographs of the Southern Cross show Gacrux as a gold jewel among blue ones, and camera sensors respond to color much as the eye does, so the contrast is no illusion of human vision. Measured through filters, Acrux is brighter in blue light than in yellow while Gacrux is far brighter in yellow, and that change of sign spans the scale from cool to hot within one small figure.

HR4763.question: Why is the top of the Southern Cross orange while its other stars are blue-white?
HR4763.why: The Southern Cross holds one warm color among its blue-white stars, and that warm star is where the scale begins.
HR4763.look: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange-red with blue-white Acrux at the foot. Defocus slightly and the color jumps out; the faint white star just north-east is a background star, not a partner.
HR4763.answer: Gacrux's surface is only about 3,700 K, under two-thirds of the Sun's, so its glow leans red; Acrux and Mimosa run above 20,000 K, which is why one small cross spans nearly the whole scale. The color told you which star was the odd one out before any spectrum did.
HR4763.story: The temperature of a red giant like Gacrux can be measured almost directly. Linked telescopes, which see detail far finer than any single one, measure the width of its tiny disk. Adding up all the light it sends us across every color then says how much each square meter of that disk gives out, which only one temperature can produce. That reading agrees with the color, which is why astronomers trust color for the countless stars too small to measure.

HR4786.question: Does a star with the Sun's pale yellow have the Sun's temperature?
HR4786.why: In the little crow the middle mark is a pale yellow star, the color of our own Sun.
HR4786.look: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Kraz is pale yellow, about the Sun's own color; compare it with orange Minkar and blue-white Gienah across the crow.
HR4786.answer: It comes close, for some 700 degrees short of the Sun's surface is near enough for the colors to match. Size is another matter, since Kraz is about 16 times the Sun's width, and color never reports that.
HR4786.story: Kraz shows roughly the color the Sun would have as a point of light at night, a shade warmer. Daylight elsewhere is set the same way: a planet around a cooler star would bask in faintly golden light and one around a hotter star in a whiter light. The eyes of anyone living there would adapt, though, and call their own sunlight plain white.

HR4853.question: Why do Mimosa and the Jewel Box's brightest stars share one icy color?
HR4853.why: On the eastern arm of the Cross, with the Jewel Box a degree away, a blue-white star shares its color with a whole cluster.
HR4853.look: Mimosa is the bright blue-white star on the eastern arm of the Cross. Put it at the edge of your view and look about 1° south-east for the Jewel Box, whose brightest stars share its icy color.
HR4853.answer: Mimosa's surface is about 27,000 K, and the Jewel Box's brightest members are hot young stars of the same kind, so the same heat paints them the same icy tint, near and far alike.
HR4853.story: Mimosa and the brightest stars of the cluster beside it are hot for the same reason: they are heavy, and a heavy star burns its fuel so fiercely that its surface runs tens of thousands of degrees. Such stars cannot last long, so a family full of them, and of their icy color, must be young.

HR4932.question: How close to the Sun's temperature is Vindemiatrix's pale yellow?
HR4932.why: Halfway up the scale the colors approach the Sun's own, and Virgo's pale yellow giant is the place to see it.
HR4932.look: Vindemiatrix sits in Virgo's northern arm, about 20 degrees west-south-west of Arcturus. In binoculars it is pale yellow; swing to Arcturus and back to see how much warmer orange looks.
HR4932.answer: Vindemiatrix runs some 750 degrees short of the Sun and as much again hotter than Arcturus, which is why it reads yellow where Arcturus reads orange. Spica, blue-white to the south, sits far higher up.
HR4932.story: Between Arcturus and Vindemiatrix the difference in heat is modest, yet the eye sees it at once when the two are compared. Their spectra say the same thing in another language: the cooler star's lines of neutral metals run stronger and the warmer star's weaker, in just the proportion that such a step in heat should produce.

HR5056.question: How hot is Spica, the blue-white star at the end of the arc from Arcturus?
HR5056.why: The arc that starts at orange Arcturus ends at a lone blue-white star, the hot end of the scale in Virgo.
HR5056.look: From Arcturus, continue the Dipper-handle curve about as far again to a lone, brilliant blue-white star. Compare its icy color with Arcturus' orange.
HR5056.answer: Spica's main star runs at about 25,300 K, nearly six times Arcturus' temperature, and most of what it gives off is ultraviolet your eyes cannot see. The blue-white that does reach you is just the long-wavelength edge of its glow.
HR5056.story: Spica's two stars orbit too closely to separate, but each leaves its own lines in the spectrum, shifting back and forth with the orbit, so astronomers can read two temperatures from one point of light. Both are hot, the brighter more so, and their blend is the icy blue-white you see.

HR509.question: Does a Sun-like star nearby look the Sun's color in binoculars?
HR509.why: To see the Sun's color at night you need a nearby star much like the Sun, and τ Ceti is one.
HR509.look: τ Ceti lies about fifteen degrees east of Diphda, the Whale's brightest star. In binoculars it is a steady pale-yellow point; swing back to Diphda, which looks more orange, to set the two marks on the scale.
HR509.answer: τ Ceti's surface is about 5,300 K, a few hundred degrees below the Sun's, so its pale yellow is very nearly the color of sunlight. Seen from a planet around τ Ceti, our Sun would be a slightly whiter star of the same kind.
HR509.story: τ Ceti is poorer in iron than the Sun, and that matters for its color in a small way, because metals crowd the blue end of a star's spectrum with dark lines. A star with fewer of them lets a little more blue escape and looks a shade whiter than its temperature alone would make it. Astronomers correct for this when they turn colors into temperatures, one reason the thermometer works as well as it does.

HR5191.question: Why is the end of the Big Dipper's handle blue-white while Dubhe glows orange?
HR5191.why: The Big Dipper's handle ends at its hottest star, the opposite end of the figure from yellow-orange Dubhe.
HR5191.look: Alkaid ends the Big Dipper's handle, crisply blue-white against yellow-orange Dubhe at the far end of the bowl. Sweep from one to the other through the white stars between.
HR5191.answer: Dubhe, at about 4,700 K, is nearly four times cooler, so the Dipper runs from orange to blue-white across one familiar shape. Most of the white stars between them sit near 9,500 K, a middle mark on the same scale.
HR5191.story: A hotter surface pays off steeply in light: the glow from each square meter climbs with the fourth power of the temperature, so doubling the heat multiplies it sixteen times. Each patch of Alkaid's surface therefore outshines an equal patch of the Sun nearly a hundredfold, and although the star is only a few times the Sun's width, it pours out hundreds of Suns' worth of light. Its tint is a measure of its power too, once you know its size.

HR5235.question: Why does Muphrid look pale yellow beside orange Arcturus?
HR5235.why: Five degrees from orange Arcturus a paler star waits, the next mark up and a star just beginning to swell.
HR5235.look: Sweep from Arcturus in Boötes about five degrees west to Muphrid. A wide field holds both: orange-gold beside pale yellow-white.
HR5235.answer: Muphrid's surface is about 6,000 K and Arcturus' about 4,300 K, so the step you see is some 1,700 degrees. As Muphrid ages and swells, its surface will cool and its color will slide toward Arcturus' orange.
HR5235.story: Muphrid and Arcturus lie only a few light-years apart, so the light of both crosses the same stretch of nearly empty space, and no dust can favor one tint over the other. That makes the pair a clean bench test: the step from orange-gold to pale yellow is the stars' own, as honest a reading as the sky offers.

HR5267.question: Why does Hadar look blue-white beside yellowish Alpha Centauri?
HR5267.why: The two Pointers make a calibration pair, and Hadar, beside Sun-like Alpha Centauri, sits at the hot end.
HR5267.look: Swing between the two Pointers, about 4° apart: Hadar is blue-white, Alpha Centauri warmer and yellower. In binoculars Hadar stays a single point, its three stars far too close to split.
HR5267.answer: Hadar's surface is about 25,000 K, more than four times Alpha Centauri's Sun-like 5,800 K, and the two Pointers show that gap as plainly as any two stars in the sky.
HR5267.story: Hadar's spectrum is rich in lines of helium, an element that only a very hot gas can make absorb light, while Alpha Centauri's is crowded with the metal lines of a Sun-like star. The two Pointers differ in their fingerprints as plainly as in their tints, and at Hadar's end of the scale it is the helium lines, not the color, that supply the number.

HR5288.question: Why is Menkent pale orange among the blue-white stars of Centaurus?
HR5288.why: Among the blue-white stars of Centaurus one giant glows warm, and it gives the scale its orange mark.
HR5288.look: Menkent is a pale orange point in binoculars, north of the brilliant stars of Centaurus. Compare it with blue-white Hadar or Spica, each about 25 degrees away, and the warmth of its tint is plain.
HR5288.answer: Its surface is about 4,850 K, a few hundred degrees short of yellow and far below Hadar's roughly 25,000 K. On the thermometer it sits at the warm end of orange.
HR5288.story: The orange of a cool star and the blue-white of a hot one leave fingerprints in their spectra too. In Menkent's light the lines of metals such as iron and calcium are strong, because its gas is cool enough for those atoms to keep their outer electrons. In Hadar's light they nearly vanish and lines of helium appear, which only a far hotter gas can excite.

HR5459.question: What color is a star with almost exactly the Sun's temperature?
HR5459.why: Every thermometer needs a calibration mark, and the brightest star of Centaurus has a member that is nearly the Sun's twin.
HR5459.look: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Its two Sun-like stars merge into one brilliant point, so compare its warm tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
HR5459.answer: Alpha Centauri A runs at about 5,800 K, the Sun's own temperature, and its light looks a warm yellow-white, with its cooler orange partner adding a touch more gold. This is the Sun's color, seen from the outside.
HR5459.story: Alpha Centauri A is so like the Sun that astronomers use it as a laboratory for our own star: its spectrum is almost a copy of sunlight, line for line. Its gentle oscillations, picked up as tiny rhythmic shifts in those lines, weigh it at about a tenth more than the Sun, so the tint you see is carried by a star of very nearly the Sun's build.

HR553.question: Why do two stars at nearly the same distance show such different colors?
HR553.why: Aries holds a white star at nearly the same distance as orange Hamal, which makes their color difference a clean test.
HR553.look: Sheratan sits in the short line of Aries, a white point in binoculars. Swing to Hamal, about four degrees north-east, and compare: white against orange.
HR553.answer: Sheratan's surface is about 8,150 K, nearly twice Hamal's 4,500 K, and with distance and dust ruled out, that gap is the whole reason for the colors. You are seeing two temperatures side by side.
HR553.story: Sheratan is really two stars, far too close for any eyepiece to split, but the Mark III interferometer on Mount Wilson resolved them and followed their eccentric orbit of about 107 days, which weighs both. The white star comes out at about twice the Sun's mass and its partner at almost exactly one Sun, with a surface very like the Sun's own. One point of light thus holds a measured case of the rule that among stars in their prime the heavier is the hotter.

HR5563.question: Why is one guardian of the pole orange and the other white?
HR5563.why: Near the pole the two guardian stars wear different colors, and the orange one adds the next mark to the scale.
HR5563.look: Between Polaris and the Big Dipper's handle shine the two guardians of the pole. In binoculars Kochab is clearly orange and Pherkad, a few degrees away, white; a touch of defocus makes the colors easier to judge.
HR5563.answer: Kochab is cool enough to glow orange, some 1,700 degrees below the Sun, while Pherkad's white means a much hotter surface. Side by side, the two guardians read as two different marks on the same thermometer.
HR5563.story: Seen from a planet around Kochab, daylight would look distinctly warm, because the star's glow peaks in the near infrared and its visible light is weighted toward red. Our Sun's glow peaks in the middle of the visible range, and eyes that evolved under it read that balanced light as white, so the orange you see in Kochab is a measure of how far its surface falls short of the Sun's.

HR5685.question: Why do some observers swear Zubeneschamali looks green?
HR5685.why: Libra's second star is famous for a color the thermometer says no star can have.
HR5685.look: Center Zubeneschamali and defocus slightly so it becomes a small disk. Compare it with white Zubenelgenubi nine degrees south-west and decide for yourself: green tinge, pale blue, or plain white?
HR5685.answer: Its surface is about 12,300 K, which places it among the blue-white stars and nowhere near a green. The green some observers report comes from contrast with nearby colors and from the way our eyes handle dim light, not from the star.
HR5685.story: Color scientists can plot every tint the human eye can perceive on a single chart, and the colors of glowing bodies at every temperature trace one curved track across it. The track runs from deep red through orange, yellow and white to a pale sky blue, and it never enters the green part of the chart at all. Put Zubeneschamali's temperature on that track and it lands among the pale blue-whites, the tint shown on its swatch.

HR5763.question: How can two matched stars in Boötes show such different colors?
HR5763.why: The ν Boötis pair sets two colors side by side in one field, and because the two look equally bright, color is the only thing left to compare.
HR5763.look: Start at Nekkar, the star at the top of the kite of Boötes, and sweep east. Binoculars show orange ν¹ and white ν² side by side, nearly equal in brightness.
HR5763.answer: ν¹ is an orange giant with a surface near 3,900 K, while ν² is a white star thousands of degrees hotter, so the pair spans much of the scale in a single field. The eye ranks them in a moment, the warm one cool and the pale one hot.
HR5763.story: Each of the ν Boötis stars has had its temperature read from its spectrum, independently of its color, and both readings agree with what your eye reports: a cool giant beside a much hotter star. The orange one is also the larger and the farther of the two, a giant whose light travels more than twice as far to arrive looking just as bright as its neighbor.

HR5793.question: What temperature does the white jewel of the Northern Crown stand for?
HR5793.why: The one bright jewel of the Northern Crown is a white mark on the scale, a sweep east of orange Arcturus.
HR5793.look: Alphecca is the one bright star in the arc of Corona Borealis, and binoculars fit the whole crown into one or two fields. It is a clean white, perhaps with a faint bluish edge; compare it with orange Arcturus, about 20° to the west.
HR5793.answer: Alphecca's surface runs at about 9,700 K, more than twice Arcturus' temperature, so its light leans to blue where Arcturus leans to orange. A smaller Sun-like companion hides in the glare, but the hot star sets the color.
HR5793.story: Alphecca sits almost exactly where Vega does on the astronomers' color scale, whose zero point was chosen so that stars of this kind come out neutral. Warmer stars such as Arcturus get positive numbers and hotter blue-white ones negative, so the scale's zero falls right at the jewel you are looking at.

HR5854.question: What does the pale orange of Unukalhai tell you about its surface?
HR5854.why: Orange comes in shades, and the serpent's heart shows a pale one, close to the point where orange gives way to yellow.
HR5854.look: Unukalhai is the brightest star of Serpens, the serpent's heart. Center it and defocus slightly to bring out its pale orange; the globular cluster M5 lies about eight degrees south-west.
HR5854.answer: Its surface is about 4,500 K, cooler than the Sun but warmer than the deep orange giants, which is why the tint is pale. A few hundred degrees more and it would read yellow.
HR5854.story: Where exactly does orange turn into yellow? There is no sharp line, because the eye blends a smooth spread of colors into one impression, and that impression shifts gradually as the peak of the glow slides out of the infrared toward the visible. Astronomers sidestep the argument by giving each star a number, its color index, and naming the color afterward.

HR5897.question: How hot is the creamy-white corner of the Southern Triangle?
HR5897.why: The Southern Triangle's creamy corner sits next to its orange one, so this step of the scale comes with its own comparison.
HR5897.look: Swing between Beta and Atria in Triangulum Australe. Atria looks a little brighter and orange, Beta creamy white.
HR5897.answer: Beta Trianguli Australis runs at about 7,200 K, roughly 3,000 degrees hotter than Atria and 1,400 hotter than the Sun. That is why Beta looks white and Atria orange, though Atria is the more powerful star.
HR5897.story: β Trianguli Australis is in its steady middle years, and stars at that stage follow a simple rule: the hotter are also the heavier, so a white tint marks a star somewhat more massive than the Sun. Atria breaks the rule only because it has left that stage and swollen, which is how a giant can be cool and bright at once.

HR591.question: How much hotter than the Sun is the creamy star of Hydrus?
HR591.why: Hydrus holds a Sun-like star and a hotter, creamier one, and this is the creamier, the white step just below the hot end.
HR591.look: Put Achernar and Alpha Hydri in the same sweep, about 5° apart. Achernar looks icy blue-white, Alpha Hydri slightly warmer and creamier.
