Mel20.answer: Each member's parallax is small and a little uncertain, but averaging nearly a thousand of them shrinks the uncertainty enormously, and the cluster comes out about 566 light-years away. With that distance fixed, the true brightness of every kind of star in it is known, ready to be laid against clusters too far for parallax.
Mel20.story: The family stands out in Gaia's data as a tight knot in motion: plot every star's drift across the sky and the cluster's members pile into one spot while the field stars scatter. Only after that sorting are the parallaxes combined, and Mirfak, measured on its own, comes out at the family's distance, which is how we know it belongs.

NGC104.question: Which of 47 Tucanae's stars are the ruler that measures it?
NGC104.why: 47 Tucanae is a brilliant globular at the edge of the Small Magellanic Cloud on the sky, a near rung and a far one touching.
NGC104.look: To the eye it is a fuzzy star beside the Small Cloud; binoculars show a round glow brightening sharply to an intense, almost starlike core. Wide binoculars hold the cluster and the Cloud's edge in one view.
NGC104.answer: Its old helium-burning stars, which share nearly one true power, and its faint Sun-like stars, matched to old neighbors measured by parallax, both set the scale. That ruler stops at the edge of our galaxy, and the Cloud behind the cluster needs a new one.
NGC104.story: The ruler stars themselves lie far beyond binoculars: each of 47 Tucanae's helium-burning stars glows at about fourteenth magnitude, around a thousand times fainter than the dimmest star your eye can catch. Only together, hundreds of thousands strong, do they make the fuzzy star you see, and telescopes pick out the helium-burning ones as a tight clump just to the red of the main band, whose level gives the depth.

NGC129.beat: A Cepheid calibrated by its cluster
NGC129.question: Why is a faint cluster in Cassiopeia part of the cosmic distance scale?
NGC129.why: The brightest member of NGC 129 is a Cepheid, and that pairing lets the cluster lend the pulsing star its distance.
NGC129.look: Look just north of the line from Caph to γ Cas for a loose patch of faint stars. Its brightest member, DL Cassiopeiae, brightens and fades over about eight days.
NGC129.answer: Measured as a crowd, NGC 129 sits about 5,800 light-years away, deep enough to test the rule on a Cepheid far from the Sun's neighborhood. Together with Hubble and Gaia parallaxes of nearer Cepheids, cluster members like DL Cas give the rule two independent footings.
NGC129.story: The cluster also checks the satellite: its members, averaged, give a far sharper shift than Gaia's single reading of the pulsing DL Cassiopeiae, so comparing the two exposes any bias in how Gaia measures such stars. That offset amounts to a few dozen millionths of an arcsecond, yet at this depth it is a few percent of the whole shift, and the expansion rate of the universe, built on Cepheids, inherits it.

NGC2451.question: Why must a yardstick cluster's members be chosen by measurement, not by eye?
NGC2451.why: NGC 2451 is a near family that carries a warning for the ladder, because what looks like one cluster here is two at different depths.
NGC2451.look: Binoculars show a bold scatter of bright stars around the orange giant c Puppis, with no visible seam between the two families. The misty glow of NGC 2477 sits about one and a half degrees away, a third cluster deeper still.
NGC2451.answer: Mix two families at different distances and the pattern of color against brightness smears out, so any distance read from it would be wrong. Sorted by Gaia's parallaxes, the nearer family becomes a clean template, and the farther one becomes a test of it.
NGC2451.story: Gaia pulls the two apart with three numbers per star, two for its drift across the sky and one for its yearly shift, about five thousandths of an arcsecond in the near family and under three in the far one. Plotted together, the stars fall into two separate knots, and only the nearer knot is averaged into a distance. The two had been taken for one cluster for centuries, a reminder that a family drawn by eye is a guess until motion and depth confirm it.

NGC2477.question: How is the misty NGC 2477 measured, when its stars barely show?
NGC2477.why: NGC 2477 shares a binocular field with the near family of NGC 2451, a ready-made contrast between a template and a cluster measured against one.
NGC2477.look: Put the bright, scattered stars of NGC 2451 at one side of the field and NGC 2477 appears at the other, a round, grainy haze. Its thousands of members are all there, merged by distance into a glow.
NGC2477.answer: Deep photographs separate its faint members, and their band of steady adult stars, matched against nearby families and corrected for dust, places NGC 2477 several times deeper than its bright neighbor. Side by side in one field, a near template and a far cluster show the whole idea of this rung at a glance.
NGC2477.story: Its aging giants offer a second ruler. Stars that have settled into burning helium in their cores gather in a tight clump of nearly equal brightness, the red clump, and in a family as rich as this one dozens of them sit together. Their faintness gives a distance that can be checked against the main-sequence fit.

NGC2516.question: Why is the Southern Beehive such a clean test of comparing clusters?
NGC2516.why: The Southern Beehive is a rich family in Carina, a natural partner for the young yardstick clusters nearby on the sky.
NGC2516.look: To the eye it is a small hazy spot; binoculars resolve dozens of stars in a patch the width of the full Moon, a few brighter ones in a rough box over a fainter haze of members.
NGC2516.answer: With age matched to the Pleiades, little but distance and a trace of dust separates its stars from their counterparts there. The fit is about as clean as this rung gets, placing the Southern Beehive about 1,300 light-years away. Clean fits like this are what let astronomers trust the method when they push it to clusters far fainter.
NGC2516.story: The fit compares like with like: in two families of the same age, stars of the same color should shine with the same power, so any gap in how bright they look is depth, plus whatever dust lies between. Toward this cluster the dust is thin, dimming its stars by only about a third of a magnitude, so the correction hardly moves the answer. With thousands of members in Gaia's census, its band is drawn so densely that the slide can be read to a few percent, and the members' own averaged shifts land in the same place.

NGC253.question: What holds up the distance to the Sculptor Galaxy, rung by rung?
NGC253.why: The Sculptor Galaxy is a bright, nearly edge-on spiral of the southern spring sky, measured with a ruler built on top of the Cepheids.
NGC253.look: From Diphda sweep about seven degrees almost due south for a faint elongated streak about the Moon's width long. From mid-northern latitudes it stays low, and averted vision lengthens it.
NGC253.answer: The ceiling its brightest red giants reach was calibrated in nearer galaxies, including the Large Magellanic Cloud, whose distances came from the rungs below. So the Sculptor Galaxy's roughly 11 million light-years still rest, step by step, on the parallax of nearby stars.
NGC253.story: The ceiling is set deep inside each old giant: its core of spent helium grows until, at almost the same weight in every such star, it ignites in a sudden flash, and the star's climb in brightness ends there. Old giants live in every galaxy, including smooth ellipticals that have no young pulsing stars at all, so this ruler works where the Cepheids cannot. In the Sculptor Galaxy, Hubble counts them in the faint halo above the bright, dusty disk, where the ceiling stands out as a sharp edge.

NGC3532.question: What can the resolved stars of the Wishing Well tell you about its depth?
NGC3532.why: The Wishing Well is a big, bright family near the Carina Nebula, close enough that binoculars show the very stars astronomers fit to the template.
NGC3532.look: About three degrees east-north-east of the Carina Nebula, binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains, with a few yellow-orange stars among the white ones.
NGC3532.answer: Its white stars, still in steady adult life, are matched color for color with nearby families, and the dimming that brings them into line puts the cluster about 1,500 light-years away. The Carina Nebula beside it lies several times deeper, so one sweep crosses two very different depths.
NGC3532.story: A clean list of members matters more than it seems: a few field stars mixed into the plot would smear the band and drag the fit. With the list cleaned, the Wishing Well's band is narrow enough that its distance from the slide can be compared with the one from Gaia's own parallaxes of its members, and the two agree.

NGC362.question: Why does NGC 362 look smaller and fainter than 47 Tucanae beside it?
NGC362.why: NGC 362 shares the Small Cloud's corner of the sky with 47 Tucanae, and stars of known power show that the two lie at very different depths.
NGC362.look: About two degrees north of the Small Cloud's main body, NGC 362 shows as a small, compact glow with a bright center, a lesser copy of 47 Tucanae.
NGC362.answer: Its stars of known power look fainter than those of 47 Tucanae by an amount that puts NGC 362 about twice as far away, so distance, more than size, makes the difference. Even so, both clusters sit well in front of the Cloud, which lies far beyond our galaxy's halo.
NGC362.story: Its stars are so numerous that Gaia can average their parallaxes into a usable value even at this depth, a geometric reading that agrees with the old helium-burning stars. Agreement this deep in the halo, by a method built for near stars, would have been unthinkable a generation ago.

NGC457.beat: A cluster lends a star its distance
NGC457.question: How can a single bright star borrow its distance from the cluster around it?
NGC457.why: The Owl Cluster is far enough that its distance rests on its many members together, and that shared distance may also belong to the bright star at its eye.
NGC457.look: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, a bright star and a fainter one form the owl's eyes, with a faint elongated spray trailing away as wings. The bright eye is φ Cassiopeiae, the star whose membership is in question.
NGC457.answer: The cluster's hundreds of members, compared with nearby templates and measured by Gaia, put it about 9,100 light-years away, and a star that truly belongs shares that depth. If φ Cas does, its modest look hides enormous power, and borrowing a distance from a cluster is exactly how rare, powerful stars like the Cepheids had their true output pinned down.
NGC457.story: Borrowing works only if membership is real, and the test is the usual pair: the star must share the cluster's distance and its motion through space. For φ Cassiopeiae the distance fits while its speed toward us is a little off the cluster's, so astronomers still hedge, and every Cepheid in a cluster had to pass the same scrutiny before it could calibrate anything.

NGC4755.beat: A cluster lends a star its distance
NGC4755.question: How does the Jewel Box turn its brightest stars into stars of known power?
NGC4755.why: The Jewel Box beside Mimosa holds a handful of rare supergiants, and on their own such stars give no hint of how far away they are or how much light they really pour out.
NGC4755.look: Just over a degree south-east of Mimosa, a compact clump shaped like a letter A is mostly blue-white, with one distinctly orange star near the middle. Its stars look faint, yet most are far more powerful than the Sun.
NGC4755.answer: Their family measures them. Matched against hot young stars of known distance, the Jewel Box's ordinary members put the cluster thousands of light-years away, far deeper than Mimosa beside it. Every supergiant born in it shares that depth, so its true output can simply be read off. Calibrated this way, rare powerful stars become rulers that reach far beyond where ordinary stars can still be seen.
NGC4755.story: A supergiant or a pulsing Cepheid found alone in the sky gives no hint of its distance, because its brightness cannot say whether it is near and modest or far and mighty. Born in a cluster, it shares a depth that hundreds of ordinary siblings have already fixed. That is why astronomers prize the few Cepheids that sit in clusters: they were among the first anchors of the rule that turns a Cepheid's beat into its power.

NGC5128.question: Why do astronomers measure Centaurus A's distance in five different ways?
NGC5128.why: Centaurus A is the nearest giant elliptical galaxy, and its distance has become a meeting point for nearly every ruler the ladder has built.
NGC5128.look: About four and a half degrees north of Omega Centauri, a dark sky shows a small, slightly oval glow, and averted vision makes it swell.
NGC5128.answer: Each ruler has its own weak spot, from dust that dims Cepheids to assumptions about old red giants, so their agreement here is the strongest evidence that the ladder is sound. Beyond this, the rulers that work best are the ones that meeting points like this calibrate.
NGC5128.story: Two of its rulers are unusual: planetary nebulae, the glowing shells cast off by dying Sun-like stars, shine in a green line of oxygen, and the brightest of them top out at nearly the same power in any galaxy. Mira stars, cool giants that pulse over a year or so, follow a period–power rule of their own. Centaurus A, with young stars in its dusty band and a vast smooth body of old ones, is one of the rare galaxies where rulers built for young stars and for old ones can all be used at once.

NGC5139.question: How many independent rulers agree on the distance to Omega Centauri?
NGC5139.why: Omega Centauri is the galaxy's heaviest globular cluster, and its distance has been measured enough ways to serve as a check on the whole halo scale.
NGC5139.look: To the eye it is a fuzzy star in Centaurus; binoculars turn it into a large, round glow brightening steadily toward the center like a snowball, its outer edge grainy under a dark sky.
NGC5139.answer: Gaia's parallaxes of its members, the motions of its stars and Hubble's studies all point to about 17,700 light-years. At that depth the halo's usual ruler, old helium-burning stars that share nearly one true power, can be checked against geometry instead of trusted blind. When independent rulers agree, astronomers can trust stars of known power to go farther.
NGC5139.story: The motion method is geometry in disguise. The stars of a swarm move at random in every direction, so their spread of speeds toward and away from us, in kilometers per second from spectra, must match their spread across the sky, measured as an angle per year. Only one distance makes the kilometers and the angles agree. For Omega Centauri thousands of stars have been measured both ways.

NGC6025.question: How far is the neat little group north of Beta Trianguli Australis?
NGC6025.why: NGC 6025 sits a few degrees from Beta Trianguli Australis, a family about as old as the Pleiades but much deeper in space.
NGC6025.look: About three degrees north of Beta Trianguli Australis, binoculars resolve a dozen or so stars in a neat group.
NGC6025.answer: Laid against templates of the same age, its stars come up short by an amount that places NGC 6025 far behind the bright star that guides you to it. A near star measured by parallax and a far cluster measured by comparison, side by side, are the ladder's first methods in one sweep.
NGC6025.story: The depth here is easy to underestimate: if Beta Trianguli Australis were a lamp across a room, five meters away, this cluster would be a cluster of lamps about three hundred meters down the road. Gaia can still average its members' shifts at that depth, and the averaged shift agrees with the comparison, but the farther a family lies, the more of the weight falls on comparing its stars with nearer ones.

NGC6067.beat: A Cepheid calibrated by its cluster
NGC6067.question: Why does a Cepheid calibration need clusters at many different depths?
NGC6067.why: NGC 6067 in Norma is a massive young cluster with Cepheids of its own, one more independent check on how a pulse reveals power.
NGC6067.look: Less than half a degree north of κ Normae, NGC 6067 is a dense, grainy patch against a crowded Milky Way. 10×50s show a few members over a fine glow.
NGC6067.answer: Calibrating with Cepheids at one depth alone would hide any error that grows with distance, such as dimming by dust, while clusters near and far, NGC 6067 at about 6,400 light-years among them, expose it. A rule tested from many angles is one astronomers can carry out of the galaxy.
NGC6067.story: This cluster holds two Cepheids that very likely share its depth, one beating in about eleven days and the other in under four, so a single cluster distance pins two quite different beats at once. Whatever the gap in their brightness, it cannot be depth, so it must be power alone, the very comparison Leavitt made in the Small Magellanic Cloud, repeated here inside our own galaxy.

NGC6087.beat: A Cepheid calibrated by its cluster
NGC6087.question: Does S Normae shine exactly as brightly as its pulse predicts?
NGC6087.why: NGC 6087 in Norma holds the Cepheid S Normae, and the cluster's own distance lets astronomers test the pulsing-star rule rather than simply trust it.
NGC6087.look: NGC 6087 shows a dozen or more stars around S Normae, the brightest and slightly yellow. Over a week or two S Nor changes by nearly a factor of two against its neighbors.
NGC6087.answer: Measured as a crowd, the cluster lies about 3,100 light-years away, and at that depth S Normae's brightness comes out where its ten-day beat says it should. Tests like this are why astronomers dare to apply the rule to Cepheids in galaxies millions of light-years away.
NGC6087.story: In the early 1950s the Cepheid scale had just been found to be badly off, and astronomers went hunting for Cepheids inside clusters, where a family's depth could fix the rule's zero point directly. S Normae, recognized as a member in the middle of that decade, was one of the first, and only a handful turned up, because Cepheids are rare and short-lived and few clusters happen to hold one at the right moment.

NGC6231.question: How is a cluster of brand-new, brilliant stars measured from thousands of light-years?
NGC6231.why: NGC 6231 is a knot of extremely young, hot stars in the Scorpion's tail, so bright that they can be seen and compared from far away.
NGC6231.look: Half a degree north of the ζ Scorpii pair, a compact knot of a dozen bright stars sits over fainter ones. Of the ζ pair, the paler, fainter star belongs to this family, while the orange one is a nearer foreground star.
NGC6231.answer: Its hottest stars, compared with hot young stars of known distance and corrected for the heavy dust in this direction, put the cluster about 5,200 light-years away. Stars this powerful stay visible far beyond the depth where ordinary stars fade, the idea the next rung takes further.
NGC6231.story: Toward this cluster the dust correction is large, and it is measured from the stars themselves: each hot star has a known true color, so how much redder it looks is how much dust lies in front. The paleness of the ζ¹ Scorpii you see is that reddening at work on a star that is really blue-hot.

NGC6397.question: What makes a nearby globular like NGC 6397 a test bed for the halo's rulers?
NGC6397.why: NGC 6397, below the Scorpion's tail, is one of the nearer globular clusters, close enough that even its faint stars can be measured in detail.
NGC6397.look: From β Arae sweep about three degrees north-east to a bright, irregular glow with a concentrated core and a ragged halo that looks grainy in steady 10×50s. From the southern hemisphere it is a highlight; from mid-northern latitudes it barely clears the horizon.
NGC6397.answer: NGC 6397 lies about 8,100 light-years away, near enough for both of the halo's rulers to be applied in detail. The old helium-burning stars that share nearly one true power and the faint Sun-like stars fitted to old neighbors measured by parallax can each check the other. Agreement in a near cluster is what lets astronomers trust the same rulers in far ones.
NGC6397.story: Its nearness lets Hubble measure even its faint Sun-like stars precisely, and those are fitted to the rare old, metal-poor neighbors of the Sun whose parallaxes are known. Hubble has also measured the cluster's own parallax directly, by sweeping its stars across the detector in long trails, a geometric value that agrees with both rulers.

NGC6752.question: What ruler reaches the Great Peacock Globular, deep in the southern halo?
NGC6752.why: The Great Peacock Globular is a bright, ancient cluster of the far-southern sky, far beyond the reach of any open-cluster template.
NGC6752.look: Binoculars show an obvious round glow with a bright, concentrated core, almost like an out-of-focus star, and a fainter halo that spreads with averted vision under a dark sky.
NGC6752.answer: Its old helium-burning stars, which every globular contains and which share nearly one true power, look faint by an amount that places it deep in the halo, and Gaia and Hubble data now add independent checks. Clusters measured this way are the last rungs inside our galaxy; the rung above them belongs to other galaxies.
NGC6752.story: This cluster is one of the first places a distance was measured with white dwarfs. The faint, dead embers of its earliest stars were matched to nearby white dwarfs of known distance, just as living stars are matched on the main sequence. Embers and living stars gave the same depth, a check that owes nothing to the helium-burning stars.

NGC752.question: How do you measure an old cluster whose brightest stars have already moved on?
NGC752.why: NGC 752 is a family more than a billion years old in Andromeda, measured by a comparison that has to allow for its age.
NGC752.look: Start at the wide orange pair 56 Andromedae and look just north-east for a large, loose patch of faint, similar stars. There is no bright center and no standout blue-white star, so let your eye relax over the whole field.
NGC752.answer: Astronomers fit only the stretch of its main sequence, the band of stars in steady adult life, that age has left untouched, where its stars match those of nearby families. The shortfall in brightness there gives about 1,400 light-years. Matching like with like, age included, is what keeps each rung honest as the ladder climbs.
NGC752.story: Its age helps the fit in one way: the stars still on the lower main sequence have had over a billion years to settle, so the band is clean and narrow, free of the still-contracting youngsters that blur young families. Its nearness helps in another, since Gaia's parallaxes of its members now check the fit directly.

NGC869.question: How far is the Double Cluster, and how was it measured before Gaia?
NGC869.why: The Double Cluster is the showpiece of this rung, two rich families thousands of light-years off whose stars can be matched, color for color, with nearby ones.
NGC869.look: Two glittering knots share one field between Cassiopeia and Perseus, each crowded with dozens of points, with a few orange supergiants among the blue-white. Those blue-white stars look faint only because of the distance; up close they would outshine the Sun enormously.
NGC869.answer: Astronomers plotted the colors and brightnesses of their stars, corrected for the dust that reddens and dims them, and slid the result onto the band set by nearby clusters. The shortfall put the pair thousands of light-years away. Gaia's averaged parallaxes now pin the pair down precisely, a firm anchor for a rung that once stood on comparison alone.
NGC869.story: The Double Cluster was a classic test of this rung because its two halves give two fits from one burst of star birth: if the slide works, both should land at the same distance, and they agree within the uncertainties. That agreement, made before Gaia existed, is part of why astronomers trusted the method far beyond the reach of parallax.

SMC.question: Leavitt's rule ranked the Cepheids; what finally told how far the Cloud is?
SMC.why: The Small Magellanic Cloud is where the pulsing-star ruler was discovered, and its own distance is a test of everything the lower rungs built.
SMC.look: Under a dark sky it looks like a small torn-off cloud, a soft, uneven glow brighter along one side, with 47 Tucanae and NGC 362 beside it like fuzzy stars.
SMC.answer: Leavitt showed only that slower Cepheids are brighter, which ranks them without measuring them, so the scale had to come from Cepheids near enough for the lower rungs, by parallax and by clusters. Today eclipsing binaries put the Cloud about 204,000 light-years away, an independent check that the ladder holds.
SMC.story: Leavitt's plot still needed a zero point, which Ejnar Hertzsprung supplied in 1913 from a few Milky Way Cepheids whose distances could only be estimated from their slow drifts across the sky. His distance to the Cloud came out many times too small. Part of the scatter in her plot was the Cloud itself, deep enough along the line of sight that its Cepheids are not all at one distance, one reason its larger, thinner neighbor later became the anchor.

STAR-Aldebaran.question: What ruler separates Aldebaran from the cluster it seems to lead?
STAR-Aldebaran.why: The ladder starts with a star measured directly, and Aldebaran comes with a built-in lesson: a star that looks like part of a family may be a stranger standing in front.
STAR-Aldebaran.look: Frame the V of the Hyades and Aldebaran sits at one tip, orange and far brighter than the cluster stars. On the sky it looks like the family's leader, and only a measurement of depth can say otherwise.
STAR-Aldebaran.answer: Parallax does it, because Aldebaran's yearly shift, about 49 thousandths of an arcsecond, is more than twice that of the cluster's stars, so it stands about 67 light-years away while the Hyades lie about 154. A cluster measured star by star in this way is exactly what the next rung needs.
STAR-Aldebaran.story: Aldebaran's motion gives it away as surely as its depth: it is receding from us faster than the cluster's members and drifting across the sky on a different heading, so it does not even travel with the family. Its distance is no abstraction either, since Pioneer 10, coasting outward in roughly its direction, would need about two million years to cover the gap. Nothing in Aldebaran's light alone could have revealed any of this; it took a measured shift and a measured motion, the two checks every later rung leans on.

STAR-Algol.question: How do we know the Demon Star is a near neighbor rather than a distant beacon?
STAR-Algol.why: Algol makes a clean first rung because its distance comes from geometry alone, with no assumption about what kind of star it is.
STAR-Algol.look: Algol is easy to the eye, a white star in Perseus that usually matches Almach in brightness and every few days sinks toward ε Persei. That brightness says nothing about distance, since a feeble star nearby and a giant far off can look exactly alike.
STAR-Algol.answer: Hipparcos watched Algol's position shift by about 36 thousandths of an arcsecond as Earth went around the Sun, and that angle puts it about 90 light-years away. Only fairly near stars give an angle this clean, so everything farther up the ladder has to be calibrated, step by step, from distances like this one.
STAR-Algol.story: The baseline for every parallax is the width of Earth's orbit, about three hundred million kilometers from one side to the other, and the angle it opens up shrinks in proportion to distance. Astronomers named their unit after it: a parsec, about 3.26 light-years, is the distance at which half that baseline spans one arcsecond, and no star lies that close. Algol sits more than twenty-five parsecs out, so its yearly swing is a small fraction of a single arcsecond, and only an instrument above the shimmering air follows it this cleanly.

STAR-Arcturus.question: What does Arcturus's distance tell you that its brightness cannot?
STAR-Arcturus.why: Arcturus opens the ladder in the spring sky, a bright star near enough that Hipparcos measured its yearly shift with little room for doubt.
STAR-Arcturus.look: Arcturus is unmistakably orange-gold in binoculars and outshines everything around it. Brightness like that could mean a modest star nearby or a giant far away, and the eye has no way to tell which.
STAR-Arcturus.answer: Its parallax, about 89 thousandths of an arcsecond, puts it about 37 light-years away, and with the distance known its brightness becomes a true power that can be compared with any other star's. Apparent brightness plus distance gives power, and every higher rung runs that sum in reverse.
STAR-Arcturus.story: Arcturus also races across the sky, more than two arcseconds a year, so its position drifts many times farther each year than its parallax wobble. Astronomers untangle the two the way you would separate a walk from a sway: the drift goes steadily one way, while the parallax loop comes back on itself every year. What is left once the drift is removed is the pure geometric shift that gives the distance.

STAR-Capella.question: How far is Capella, and why can that number be trusted?
STAR-Capella.why: Capella opens the ladder with a distance measured as directly as anything in astronomy, by the shift that Earth's own orbit produces.
STAR-Capella.look: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star leading Auriga, high overhead on winter evenings. It outshines everything around it, and brightness like that is a hint of closeness, but not yet a measurement.
STAR-Capella.answer: Hipparcos measured a yearly shift of about 76 thousandths of an arcsecond, which puts Capella about 43 light-years away, and the only assumption behind that number is the size of Earth's orbit. Stars measured this cleanly become reference points for how bright each kind of star truly is, the knowledge the next rungs depend on.
STAR-Capella.story: Capella offers a rare second route to its distance. Its two stars have been tracked both in angle, by interferometers, and in speed, from the Doppler shift of their light. The speeds give the orbit's true size in kilometers, the interferometers give its size in arcseconds, and the ratio of the two is the distance. That orbital parallax agrees with the satellite's yearly shift, two independent rulers meeting on one star.

STAR-Procyon.question: Procyon looks less dazzling than Sirius; is it farther away, weaker, or both?
STAR-Procyon.why: Procyon is a near neighbor whose distance comes straight from its yearly shift, which makes it a natural first rung for the winter sky.
STAR-Procyon.look: Procyon is the creamy-white eastern corner of the Winter Triangle, clearly fainter than Sirius to the south. Hold both in mind and ask how much of the difference is distance.
STAR-Procyon.answer: It is both a little farther and genuinely weaker, since its parallax of about 285 thousandths of an arcsecond places it about 11 light-years away, just beyond Sirius, and distance alone cannot explain the whole gap. Separating distance from true power this way is the trick the ladder keeps reusing all the way up.
STAR-Procyon.story: The arithmetic is satisfying to do yourself: compare how much fainter one star looks with how much farther it lies, and whatever the distance cannot explain must be a difference in true power. Light fades with the square of distance, so a star twice as far looks a quarter as bright, and any shortfall beyond that belongs to the star itself. Distance first, power second: that order of reasoning is the one every rung keeps.

STAR-Sirius.question: Is Sirius the brightest star because it is powerful, or because it is close?
STAR-Sirius.why: The first rung should be a star near enough that its distance comes from geometry alone, and few bright stars are nearer than Sirius.
STAR-Sirius.look: Sirius blazes white below Orion, flickering through colors when it is low. Its glare is so strong that it is tempting to think it must be enormous, so hold that thought until the distance is known.
STAR-Sirius.answer: Sirius looks so bright mostly because it is close, since its parallax of about 379 thousandths of an arcsecond puts it among the very nearest stars you can see by eye. Knowing the distance turns apparent brightness into true power, and that conversion is the tool every higher rung depends on.
STAR-Sirius.story: In the 1690s Christiaan Huygens, assuming Sirius was a twin of the Sun, let sunlight through a tiny hole until it looked as faint as the star, and concluded it lay about twenty-eight thousand times farther than the Sun. The true distance is about twenty times greater, and much of the gap comes from that one assumption, since Sirius pours out roughly twenty-five Suns' worth of light. Brightness yields a distance only once power is known, and parallax is the first ruler that needs no such guess.

STAR-Vega.question: How long has Vega's light been on its way, and how do we know?
STAR-Vega.why: The ladder starts with a star close enough to measure by geometry, and Vega, overhead on summer nights, is one of the brightest of them.
STAR-Vega.look: Vega is the hard blue-white spark of Lyra, ringed in binoculars by faint stars the eye alone misses. Most of those faint stars lie far beyond it, the distant backdrop against which a near star's shift is measured.
STAR-Vega.answer: Hipparcos measured Vega shifting by about 130 thousandths of an arcsecond against that backdrop, which puts it about 25 light-years away, so the light you see set out about 25 years ago. Once a handful of such distances are secure, the true brightness of stars like Vega is known, and that is the calibration the next rung borrows.
STAR-Vega.story: Vega was one of the three stars that opened the field in the late 1830s: Friedrich Struve measured its shift at almost the same time as Bessel caught 61 Cygni and Thomas Henderson Alpha Centauri. His first value was remarkably close to today's, though he later revised it in the wrong direction, a reminder of how hard these tiny angles were to trust at the eyepiece.

Stock2.question: Before Gaia, how could anyone measure a cluster too far for a clean parallax?
Stock2.why: Stock 2 is a big, loose family beside the Double Cluster, close enough that binoculars show many of the very stars the comparison uses.
Stock2.look: Stock 2 fills much of the field two degrees north of the Double Cluster, a loose spray in which some observers trace a little muscleman. Its stars look modest, yet many of them are hotter and more powerful than the Sun, dimmed only by distance.
Stock2.answer: Plot its steady adult stars by color and brightness, the band astronomers call the main sequence, and slide it until it lines up with the same band in a cluster of known distance; the amount of sliding is the distance. The method works at any depth where the stars can still be seen, which is how the ladder outruns parallax. Gaia's parallaxes have since checked the slide, and it holds.
Stock2.story: This family is a hard case for the method because of its sprawl. Its members cover more sky than several full Moons, mixed with thousands of unrelated stars in front and behind, which blur any plot of its colors and brightnesses. Before Gaia sorted members by their motions, any fit here had to guess at membership, and Gaia's census is what turned a loose sprinkle into a measured family.

lenses.storyline: Stars are never born alone. A collapsing cloud makes hundreds or thousands of them in one burst, siblings that share a birthday, a makeup and a motion through space, and an open cluster is simply such a family seen while it is still together. Every journey of this theme follows what time does to a family. Siblings born on the same day do not age at the same pace: the heaviest burn through their fuel first, so the first member to swell into an orange giant becomes the family's clock. Meanwhile passing clouds and the steady tidal pull of the Milky Way peel members away, until old families are thin, wide or dissolving, and only the heaviest last for billions of years. In the end the siblings are scattered across whole constellations, and the only tie left is that they still travel the same way, which is exactly how the Sun's own family, long since dispersed, would look today.

AST-Hyades.question: How much of the Hyades family is still held together by its own gravity?
AST-Hyades.why: The Hyades are the nearest star family of all, and an old one, so this is where you can watch a family thinning out with your own eyes.
AST-Hyades.look: Sweep along the two arms of the Bull's V-shaped face; the family is too big for one field. Among its white and yellowish members a few are tinted orange, its aged giants, while bright orange Aldebaran at one tip is an outsider standing in front.
AST-Hyades.answer: Gravity still holds only part of the family. Gaia counts nearly a thousand members, yet only about 190 Suns' worth of stars is still within the cluster's gravitational grip, and the rest are working their way out into the Milky Way. At about 625 million years, the Hyades are a family in their last chapters as a cluster.
AST-Hyades.story: The Hyades are near enough for every member to be placed in three dimensions. Astronomers can therefore draw the boundary where the family's own gravity gives way to the galaxy's tide, about 26 light-years from the center, and simply count who lies inside it. A large share of the family already lies outside, on its way out, and the members still gathered near the middle are mostly the heavier ones. In a family that has lived this long, the lightest siblings are always the first to be pushed to the edge and lost.

AST-OrionBelt.question: Will the Belt stars and their young siblings stay together as they age?
AST-OrionBelt.why: Orion's Belt marks the heart of a young family of a different kind from a cluster: hot, heavy siblings spread across several degrees of sky, the brightest family of the winter sky.
AST-OrionBelt.look: Put the middle Belt star at the center and let the outer two sit near the edges. An S-shaped chain of fainter stars winds through the field, and many of them share the Belt stars' blue-white color and their birth.
AST-OrionBelt.answer: These siblings will not stay together. An association like this is born too loose for its own gravity to hold, so they are already drifting apart while only a few million years old. In time they will spread across whole constellations, tied together only by the direction they travel.
AST-OrionBelt.story: That a group like this is flying apart was shown by its motions. In the 1950s Adriaan Blaauw found that the stars of such associations move outward from a common center, like fragments of a slow explosion. Running the motions backward gave the time since they were together, a second clock alongside the ages read from the stars themselves. Gaia has since measured those motions for thousands of members across Orion and found the same pattern, branch by branch.

Cr69.beat: Born together: a family in a swept bubble
Cr69.question: What might happen to a young star family if one of its members explodes?
Cr69.why: The little cluster around Meissa, at Orion's head, is a young family that has already lost its cloud, and it shows that a family's early life can be violent as well as shared.
Cr69.look: Aim at Orion's head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix, and the faint smudge becomes a neat triangle with a dozen fainter siblings around it. There is no glow at all; the space around this family has been swept clean.
Cr69.answer: It is left standing in the open. An explosion like that, together with the light of the hot young stars, may well be what drove the leftover gas out into a ring wide enough to frame Orion's head in photographs. A family stripped of its gas has only its own gravity, about 360 Suns' worth, to keep it together.
Cr69.story: A cloud turns only a small share of its gas into stars, often less than a third, so in its first few million years a young family is held together mostly by gas that is not stars at all. When that gas is blown away, the gravity holding the siblings drops suddenly, and stars that were orbiting comfortably are left moving too fast to be held. Most newborn families come apart this way, and the survivors are those that turned an unusually large share of their cloud into stars.

DS-MizarAlcor.question: Do Mizar and Alcor belong to a bigger family than just each other?
DS-MizarAlcor.why: Mizar and Alcor are the famous pair in the Big Dipper's handle, and they are part of the clearest example of scattered siblings in the northern sky.
DS-MizarAlcor.look: Center the middle star of the Dipper's handle with Alcor beside it, then sweep along the handle and across the bowl. Mizar, Alioth, Megrez, Phecda and Merak share one white color, while Dubhe at the bowl's far corner is yellow-orange.
DS-MizarAlcor.answer: They belong to a much bigger family. The pair moves through space in step with Merak, Phecda, Megrez and Alioth, all born together about 414 million years ago. That family has since spread over some twenty degrees of sky, and only its shared motion still marks them as kin.
DS-MizarAlcor.story: The Dipper's family reaches far beyond the Dipper. Stars that share its motion are found all around the sky, because the Sun happens to sit inside the scattered outskirts of the group, and Sirius is often counted among them, though that claim is debated. Only the core still gathers in the Dipper, a handful of bright stars that have stayed close enough to look like a pattern.

HR1712.question: How far can a star travel from its family in two and a half million years?
HR1712.why: AE Aurigae looks like an ordinary faint star near M38, but it was born in Orion, and it shows the most dramatic way a family can lose a member.
HR1712.look: From M38 drift about three degrees west-south-west to the lone, brighter star there. Nothing in the view marks it as unusual; its family tie is written entirely in its motion.
HR1712.answer: It can cross a good part of the sky. Flung out of the Orion Nebula's young cluster at high speed, AE Aurigae has covered hundreds of light-years and now shines among the stars of Auriga, far from any sibling. Its partner in flight, μ Columbae, left at the same moment in the opposite direction.
HR1712.story: Stars are thrown out of families in two ways. In one, a heavy partner explodes and its companion, suddenly released, flies off at its orbital speed. In the other, a close encounter among several stars in a crowded young cluster flings one outward while the rest tighten into a closer pair. AE Aurigae is the textbook case of the second kind, because the tightened pair it left behind can still be found in Orion's Sword.

HR1931.beat: Born together: a household within a family
HR1931.question: Is the bright star σ Orionis one sibling, or a whole household of them?
HR1931.why: σ Orionis sits at the center of one of Orion's youngest families, about three million years old, and it shows how tightly some newborn siblings stay bound.
HR1931.look: From Alnitak drop about a degree south-west to a small knot of stars. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east, and the scatter of faint stars around it is the rest of its family.
HR1931.answer: It is a whole household. At least three heavy siblings are locked in orbit within that one point, while the cluster's lighter members spread around them. The tighter such a bond, the longer it survives what time does to the rest of the family.
HR1931.story: Telling σ Orionis's siblings from the stars in front of and behind it relies on the marks of youth. Very young stars of modest mass still hold the lithium they were born with, flare brightly in X-rays and are often still wrapped in dusty disks that glow in the infrared. A faint star near σ Orionis that shows all three is almost certainly kin. Counted this way the family runs to a few hundred members, most of them far too faint for binoculars.

HR1996.question: Where is μ Columbae's partner in flight now?
HR1996.why: μ Columbae is a faint star in the Dove, south of Orion, and the family it came from lies far to the north, in Orion's Sword.
HR1996.look: From Phact, the brightest star of Columba, nudge about two degrees north-east to the faint bluish-white star there. Its color matches the hot young stars of Orion's Sword, the family it left.
HR1996.answer: Its partner is AE Aurigae, on the other side of Orion in Auriga, flung out of the same young cluster in the opposite direction. Two siblings born in one nest now sit on opposite sides of the constellation that made them.
HR1996.story: Tracing μ Columbae home works only because it moves so fast. Like the partner it left with, it flies at around a hundred kilometers a second relative to its surroundings, many times the gentle drift of ordinary stars, so its path stands out clearly against the background. The Hipparcos satellite's precise motions let astronomers run both paths back to a single point and a single moment. Slower escapees from the same nursery have surely left too, but their trails are lost among the drifting stars of Orion.

HR2020.beat: Scattered: a family named for one star
HR2020.question: Why does a star only 23 million years old stand alone, with no family around it?
HR2020.why: Beta Pictoris is famous for the planet-forming disk around it, but it is also the namesake of a whole family of young stars.
HR2020.look: Sweep about six degrees west of Canopus to a lone, modest white star in an empty-looking area. Nothing in the view hints at its family, and that emptiness is the point.
HR2020.answer: It does have a family, just not a cluster: Beta Pictoris gives its name to a moving group of young stars born with it about 23 million years ago. They are now spread so widely across the sky that only their shared motion shows they belong together. Its siblings are scattered far beyond any binocular field.
HR2020.story: The family's age has been measured with two different clocks. Its faint red members still show lithium down to a sharp boundary, the same test used in clusters. The members' motions, run backward, draw together into a smaller region some twenty million years ago, and the two answers agree fairly well. As the nearest family this young, its members are among the best places to look for planets still glowing with the heat of their formation.

HR4295.question: Which of the Big Dipper's stars are Merak's true siblings?
HR4295.why: Merak, the lower pointer of the Big Dipper, belongs to a family that no longer looks like one: its siblings are spread across the whole pattern.
HR4295.look: Sweep from Merak across the bowl to Phecda and Megrez and out along the handle to Alioth and Mizar. All five are white and of similar brightness, a family resemblance; Dubhe, the upper pointer just five degrees from Merak, is yellow-orange.
HR4295.answer: Its true siblings are Phecda, Megrez, Alioth and Mizar with Alcor: together with Merak they drift across the sky at the same rate in the same direction, the signature of a shared birth about 414 million years ago. Dubhe and Alkaid, the two ends of the Dipper, are passers-by, and Dubhe lies half again as far away as Merak.
HR4295.story: The five Dipper siblings are no longer bound to one another, but they set out with nearly the same velocity, and small differences in speed take hundreds of millions of years to pull siblings far apart. Over the next hundred thousand years or so the Dipper's outline will warp, as Dubhe and Alkaid go their own ways, while these five keep traveling together.

HR4656.question: Are the stars of the Southern Cross a family, or only a pattern?
HR4656.why: δ Crucis, the faintest star of the Cross, belongs to a family that was born together and has since spread out over several constellations.
HR4656.look: Take in the whole Cross in one or two fields. δ Crucis, Mimosa and Acrux share a blue-white color, while Gacrux at the top glows orange; color is the one family trait you can actually see.
HR4656.answer: They are mostly a family. δ Crucis and Mimosa, and probably Acrux, share the motion of the Lower Centaurus–Crux group, while orange Gacrux is a nearer stranger that only lines up with them. The family's other members are scattered across Centaurus and beyond, still drifting the same way.
HR4656.story: The Cross's family is one branch of the largest family of young stars near the Sun, the Scorpius–Centaurus association, which stretches from Scorpius through Centaurus to Crux and holds thousands of members. Its main branches differ in age by several million years, the youngest in Scorpius, as if star birth had moved through the region in stages, and Gaia now splits even those branches into smaller groups.

HR4853.beat: Scattered: a loose sibling beside a tight family
HR4853.question: Why did Mimosa's family scatter while the Jewel Box, born at the same time, did not?
HR4853.why: Mimosa sits a degree from the Jewel Box and is about the same age, which makes this one field the clearest comparison of a family that held together and one that did not.
HR4853.look: Put Mimosa at the edge of the field and look about a degree south-east for the tight knot of the Jewel Box. Both share the same icy blue-white: one a lone sibling, the other a family still packed together.
HR4853.answer: The two families were born differently. The Jewel Box formed as a dense knot of thousands of stars whose combined gravity still holds it. Mimosa's family was born as a loose association that gravity never bound, so its members have been drifting apart from the start.
HR4853.story: Whether a birth ends in a cluster or a loose association seems to depend on how dense the gas was. Where the cloud was packed tightly, stars formed fast and close together, and their combined gravity held on after the gas cleared; where it was spread thin, the stars formed in a loose web that was never bound at all. Surveys of nearby star-forming regions find most young stars in the loose kind, which is why scattered families outnumber clusters.

HR5469.beat: Scattered: a branch of the Scorpius family
HR5469.question: How far across the sky do the siblings of the Scorpius stars reach?
HR5469.why: α Lupi is a hot blue-white giant in Lupus, far from any cluster, and its family is spread so widely that no single view could ever frame it.
HR5469.look: Find the clean blue-white star in a rich, scattered field south-west of Scorpius. Its color matches the bright stars of the Scorpion's head; that likeness, and a shared drift too slow to see, are all that mark it as kin.
HR5469.answer: They reach across a quarter of the southern sky. α Lupi belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, an older branch of the same great family as the Scorpius stars, now spread from Lupus to Centaurus. This is what a family looks like once nothing binds it.
HR5469.story: This scattered family may have touched the Earth. Its heaviest members have been exploding for millions of years, and the blasts are thought to have helped hollow out the bubble of thin, hot gas the Sun now sits in. Radioactive iron laid down on the deep sea floor a few million years ago is often traced to supernovae in this very group. A family can be strewn across the sky and still leave its mark on its neighbors.

IC1396.beat: Born together: still in the nest
IC1396.question: Is a star family born all at once, or does it arrive in waves?
IC1396.why: Trumpler 37, the cluster at the heart of IC 1396, is a family caught while it is still being born, the earliest frame of a family's life that binoculars can reach.
IC1396.look: Put the deep-orange Garnet Star at the north edge of the field and find the scatter of stars around HD 206267 to its south-south-west. Under a dark sky a faint glow may hang around them, the remains of the family's cloud.
IC1396.answer: It arrives in waves. Its sub-clusters have slightly different ages averaging about 4 million years, and at the cloud's edge the youngest siblings are still forming, squeezed into being by their elders. A family's birthday is really a birth season, short beside everything that comes after.
IC1396.story: Telling a birth season from a single birthday needs a clock for stars only a few million years old. Newborn stars of modest mass are still contracting toward their adult size, so at a given temperature a younger one is larger and brighter. Plotting the members' brightness against their color therefore shows how much their ages differ. In this family the scatter is real, a sign that its siblings arrived over a stretch of time rather than all at once.

IC2602.beat: Born together: one of a pair of litters
IC2602.question: Was the Southern Pleiades born alone, or alongside other star families?
IC2602.why: The Southern Pleiades are one of the nearest star families to the Sun, a spray of young siblings around Theta Carinae, and they open the family story in the far-southern sky.
IC2602.look: Center Theta Carinae and let the two or three dozen members spread over about a degree around it. They are nearly all blue-white, with no orange point among the bright ones, the look of a family that is still young.
IC2602.answer: It was born alongside others. The Omicron Velorum Cluster in Vela lies at the same distance, about 490 light-years, and has nearly the same age, so the two families probably came out of the same corner of one star-forming region. Clouds tend to make families in batches, and batches drift apart.
IC2602.story: Clouds big enough to make star families are themselves clumpy, with many dense knots scattered through a complex hundreds of light-years across, and each knot can collapse into a family of its own. Families born from one complex share a chemistry and a general drift through the galaxy, so astronomers look for clusters with matching ages, distances and motions as signs of a common origin. Over tens of millions of years the galaxy's rotation stretches such a batch apart, until the sibling clusters lie in different constellations.

IC4651.beat: Thinning out: compact against the odds
IC4651.question: How has IC 4651 stayed compact for 1.7 billion years?
IC4651.why: IC 4651 is about as old as NGC 6208 and lies in the same corner of the sky, yet it still looks like a proper cluster, an old family that has kept its shape.
IC4651.look: From α Arae sweep about one degree west for a small, rich group of faint stars; averted vision fills it in. Its compactness, not its brightness, is what stands out.
IC4651.answer: It has stayed compact by being heavy enough: about 2,300 Suns' worth of stars, roughly twice the mass of NGC 6208 nearby, which has thinned to a sprinkle at a similar age. For an old family, weight is what decides whether it keeps its shape or fades into the galaxy.
IC4651.story: Weight is not the only thing that decides a family's fate. Clusters that orbit far from the galaxy's crowded inner disk, or that ride above its thin layer of gas, meet fewer of the giant clouds that do most of the damage, so two families of equal weight can age very differently. Astronomers use Gaia's motions to trace each cluster's orbit back and estimate how rough its life has been.

IC4665.beat: Born together: a young family near home
IC4665.question: How young is the family of white stars beside Cebalrai compared with its neighbors?
IC4665.why: IC 4665 is a young family only about 1,100 light-years away, and it begins a line of three clusters along the Milky Way from Ophiuchus into Serpens that differ mainly in age.
IC4665.look: Center Cebalrai, the orange shoulder star of Ophiuchus, and move a degree north-east to a ragged group of white stars wider than the full Moon. Count the brighter members: none has the warm tint of an aged star.
IC4665.answer: It is young, somewhere between 30 and 60 million years old, about a tenth the age of NGC 6633 ten degrees to the east. The two lie at similar distances, so the difference between them is time alone, and IC 4665 is the version before time has done its work.
IC4665.story: A family's age can be read from the top of its membership. The heaviest stars burn through their core hydrogen soonest, so the heaviest member still in its steady adult life marks how long the family has lived. Here, hot blue-white stars several times the Sun's mass are still in their prime. That caps the family's age, and the faint end, where small stars slowly destroy their lithium, gives a matching answer from below.

IC4756.beat: Thinning out: the oldest of three
IC4756.question: How much of IC 4756's family still holds together after 840 million years?
IC4756.why: IC 4756 is the oldest of the three families strung along the Milky Way from Ophiuchus into Serpens, and it shows the stage that IC 4665 and NGC 6633 are heading for.
IC4756.look: From θ Serpentis at the tip of the snake's tail, sweep about four degrees west to a broad scatter of faint stars over two full-Moon widths. Its edges fade into the Milky Way; let your eye find the slightly denser middle.
IC4756.answer: Over 700 members still move together, about a thousand Suns' worth in all. Yet the edges you saw blending into the Milky Way are a fair picture of the family: thinned, wide and slowly giving its members back to the galaxy.
IC4756.story: Because the three families lie at broadly similar distances and behind similar dust, their charts of color against brightness can be laid directly on top of one another. The band of stars still burning core hydrogen is the same in all three, but it ends lower and lower as age increases. The youngest still holds bright blue-white members, while in the oldest the band bends away among stars only a couple of times the Sun's mass. That overlay is the experiment the three clusters make together.

M103.beat: Born together: one of a brood of clusters
M103.question: Can whole star clusters be born together, like siblings themselves?
M103.why: M103 is one of several young clusters that the Perseus spiral arm made in the same stretch of gas, so it lets you see family on two scales at once: stars that are siblings, in clusters that are cousins.
M103.look: Find the small, wedge-shaped knot a degree from Ruchbah, then sweep east toward NGC 663. Several small grainy patches share this part of the Milky Way, each a separate family born from the same arm.
M103.answer: Whole clusters can be born together, and M103 is traditionally grouped with NGC 654, NGC 659 and NGC 663 as one association. These are clusters born from neighboring parts of a single star-forming complex, all within a few tens of millions of years. That looser, larger family is held together by nothing, and it is the first to come apart.
M103.story: Star formation is clumpy at every scale: a giant cloud breaks into dense knots, each knot into smaller cores, and each core into a few stars, so siblings come grouped within groups. The tightest knots, rich enough to stay bound, become clusters like this one, while the looser material between them makes stars that drift off almost at once. That is why clusters born together sit in a wider haze of scattered stars of the same age, a family tree you can see as a pattern on the sky.

M11.beat: Thinning out: too heavy to scatter quickly
M11.question: Why does the Wild Duck's family stay packed together while others spread out?
M11.why: The Wild Duck is a family a few hundred million years old that shows almost no sign of thinning, the exception that explains the rule.
M11.look: Two degrees south-east of β Scuti, in the bright Scutum star cloud, find a compact, fan-shaped haze with a brighter star at its apex. It looks granular in 10×50s: thousands of siblings still packed tightly.
M11.answer: Its own weight holds it: with thousands of stars crammed close together, its gravity outmatches the galaxy's pull far better than a family of a few hundred could. Most families are born much lighter, which is why most of them come apart, and even the Wild Duck will thin in the end, only far more slowly.
M11.story: What protects a family from the galaxy's pull is how tightly it is packed compared with the reach of that pull. The galaxy's tide sets an outer boundary beyond which a member belongs to the galaxy rather than the family, and in a heavy, compact cluster that boundary lies far outside the crowded core, so few stars wander near it. A light, sprawling family fills its boundary to the brim, and every nudge spills members over the edge.

M16.beat: Born together: a family racing its own light
M16.question: Can a family keep having siblings while its eldest tear the nursery apart?
M16.why: The cluster in the Eagle Nebula is a family a few million years old whose heaviest members are already eroding the cloud they came from, the most hurried stage of family life.
M16.look: Find the tight scatter of a dozen or so stars in a soft glow; under a dark sky averted vision shows the haze brighter on one side. You are looking at the family and the remains of its nest together.
M16.answer: The family keeps growing for a while: inside the dense pillars that resist the glare, stars are still forming, and they must finish before the light boils their cradle away. A family's birth is a few million years of overlapping arrivals, and then the doors close for good.
M16.story: Inside the pillars, infrared cameras that see through dust have found young stars still wrapped in their cocoons. At the pillar tips sit small dense knots, nicknamed evaporating gaseous globules, some of them holding a forming star. A star caught in one of those knots when the light strips it bare stops growing where it is, so the cluster's glare may decide not only how many siblings the family gets but how heavy they end up.

M23.question: Will the newborn star families of Sagittarius ever look like M23?
M23.why: M23 lies a few degrees from the Lagoon and the other young families of Sagittarius, but it is a few hundred million years older, the same kind of family well past its youth.
M23.look: Hop about four and a half degrees north-west from μ Sagittarii to a broad cloud of faint stars crossed by curving chains, with a brighter star off one edge. Averted vision brings out many more members, all of a similar, modest brightness.
M23.answer: Some will, if they are heavy enough: M23 has kept its family together because it was born rich, while lighter litters now forming nearby will mostly have dissolved into the Milky Way long before they reach its age.
M23.story: Counts of clusters by age show how few make it this far. Young families still embedded in their clouds are common, but families tens of millions of years old are far rarer. Astronomers estimate that only around one newborn cluster in ten survives its first ten million years as a recognizable group. Families of this age are the rare survivors of that early sorting, and they keep thinning slowly afterward.

M25.beat: First to age: the restless sibling
M25.question: Why is the one restless star in M25 among the family's heaviest members?
M25.why: M25 is a family about 100 million years old with one member that refuses to keep still, and that restlessness is a sign of age, not youth.
M25.look: Hop about four and a half degrees east-north-east from μ Sagittarii to a loose group of bright stars spread over half a degree. U Sagittarii is one of the central stars; compare it with its neighbors and note it as the one that changes over a week.
M25.answer: Only heavy stars reach that stage this early: U Sagittarii has used up the hydrogen in its core and is crossing a brief, unstable phase on its way to old age, which makes it pulse. Its siblings, lighter and slower to age, still shine steadily around it.
M25.story: Cepheids are a passing phase. After a heavy star leaves its steady life and swells, it may loop back toward hotter temperatures while it burns helium, and whenever it crosses a narrow band of temperatures its outer layers begin to pulse. Only stars of several Suns make that loop, so finding a Cepheid in a cluster says the family's heaviest stars have just come of age, a clock read from one restless member.

M29.question: How much of a brilliant newborn family can a cloud of dust hide?
M29.why: M29 is a young family of hot, heavy stars, but it lies behind the dust of the Cygnus Rift.
M29.look: Center Sadr, at the middle of the Northern Cross, and drop about two degrees south. A compact knot of five or six stars sits in a small box shape, faint but distinct against the Milky Way.
M29.answer: It can hide most of its glory: the Rift's dust dims M29 more than tenfold, turning a family of brilliant young stars into a faint little box. Behind the veil, though, it is a textbook newborn litter, every bright member still hot and in its prime.
M29.story: The surest sign of a very young family is that its heaviest members are still alive. Stars a dozen or more times the Sun's mass last only some tens of millions of years, so a cluster whose brightest members are of that hot kind cannot be old, however faint the dust makes it look. Spectra cut through the dimming, since the lines that mark a hot star survive the reddening, and that is how a faint little box was recognized as a newborn family.

M3.beat: Thinning out: too heavy ever to scatter
M3.question: Can a star family be heavy enough never to come apart at all?
M3.why: M3 is a star family in a completely different weight class from the open clusters, and an extreme test of how much a family's weight matters.
M3.look: A little past halfway from Cor Caroli toward Arcturus, find an obvious round glow, brighter toward the middle. It will not break into stars in binoculars: its siblings crowd far too closely to separate.
M3.answer: A family can come very close: M3 has kept hundreds of thousands of siblings together for most of the age of the universe. It manages this because its gravity dwarfs anything an open cluster can muster and its orbit keeps it out in the halo, far from the crowded disk where lighter families are torn apart. The Sun's family, like almost every family, was born far lighter.
M3.story: Even a family this heavy leaks. In the crowded core, close passes now and then fling a star out fast enough to escape, and each crossing of the galaxy's disk squeezes the cluster and loosens a few more. So globular clusters slowly shed members too, a few at a time over billions of years. Some lighter ones have already dissolved completely, and their stars, drawn out into long streams, now belong to the galaxy's halo.

M34.beat: Thinning out: losing members one by one
M34.question: Where are M34's missing members going?
M34.why: M34 is a family a couple of hundred million years old, past its youth and slowly losing members, the stage at which most clusters begin to fade into the galaxy.
M34.look: Roughly halfway between Algol and Almach, find the loose group of a dozen or so stars, several in pairs, over a fainter glitter. Count the stars you are sure of; most of the family lies beyond what binoculars can show.
M34.answer: They are going out into the Milky Way. Passing gas clouds and the galaxy's tidal pull tug members away a few at a time, and each escapee keeps drifting along close to M34's own path, a sibling that has left home but still travels in the family's direction.
M34.story: Escape is slow and mostly quiet. Inside the family, members constantly trade energy in gentle gravitational encounters. Now and then one ends up just fast enough to climb past the edge of the cluster's grip, after which the galaxy's tide carries it off. Gaia sees the result as a sparse halo of members well outside the cluster's visible core, siblings on their way out.

M35.beat: Born together: a Pleiades-age family far away
M35.question: Would a family like the Pleiades still look like a family from six times farther?
M35.why: M35 was born at about the same time as the Pleiades, so it is the same kind of family seen from much farther off, a test of what we can still recognize as kin at a distance.
M35.look: Find the round, grainy glow at Gemini's feet with resolved stars sprinkled across it. The sprinkle is the family's brightest members; the grain behind them is hundreds more, too faint to separate.
M35.answer: Such a family would still read as one, though only just: at about 2,700 light-years only the brightest siblings stand out, and the rest blur into a glow. The small smudge of NGC 2158 beside it shows how much depth one field can hide, for it is a much older family far behind and no relation at all.
M35.story: At this distance a single star's parallax is too small to settle whether it belongs, but motion is more forgiving. Members drift across the sky together, so in a plot of every star's motion the family stands out as a tight clump while foreground and background stars scatter widely. That is how Gaia picked hundreds of siblings out of a crowded winter field. The same plot shows the small cluster beside it drifting another way, the mark of a stranger.

M36.beat: Born together: nobody has aged yet
M36.question: What does a star family look like before any of its members has grown old?
M36.why: M36 is the youngest of Auriga's three bright clusters and the baseline for the other two: a family photographed before time has changed any of its members.
M36.look: Find the small, compact patch with several stars popping out of it. Its brightest members share one blue-white, with no warmer, orange point among them.
M36.answer: It looks exactly like this: a tight knot whose brightest stars are still hot and in their prime, because even the heaviest siblings have not yet run out of hydrogen in their cores. A few degrees away in Auriga, older families show what comes next.
M36.story: Neighbors on the sky are not necessarily kin. M36 and the other two bright clusters of Auriga lie at broadly similar depths, yet their ages differ by hundreds of millions of years. They are separate families sharing a stretch of the galaxy's disk, not sisters from one cloud. Age is the test that separates neighbors from relatives, and the youngest of the three shows what the other two looked like when they were new.

M37.beat: First to age: a family of orange elders
M37.question: Where did M37's heaviest siblings go?
M37.why: M37 is the oldest of Auriga's three bright clusters, the family that has gone furthest down the road its younger neighbors are just starting on.
M37.look: Find the rich, even glow south-east of M36, like a ball of fine sugar with only a handful of points resolved. The few that stand out are the family's aged giants; the sugar is thousands of quieter siblings.
M37.answer: Many are still there, but dark: many of its heavier members have died and left white dwarfs, cooling embers far too faint for binoculars, while the next heaviest are the orange giants that now lead the family. A family about half a billion years old has already lost its first generation of elders.
M37.story: The dead siblings are not lost to science. Deep images find this family's white dwarfs as faint points, and their masses, read from their spectra, can be matched to the masses of the stars that made them. That works because in a family of known age only stars above a certain weight have had time to die. That matching is how astronomers learned how much of a star is left behind when it dies, a recipe that applies to the Sun as well.

M38.beat: First to age: the sparkle gone
M38.question: Is M38 an older sibling of M36, or a stranger from another generation?
M38.why: M38 lies at almost the same distance as M36, which makes the pair a fair comparison of two families seen at different ages.
M38.look: From M36 move about two and a half degrees north-west. M38 is bigger and softer, a grainy cloud rather than a bright knot; switch between the two and compare their sparkle.
M38.answer: It is a stranger from another generation: born roughly 270 million years ago against M36's 22 million, it came out of a different cloud long before. Its top siblings have already aged away, which is why the bigger family now shines so much more quietly.
M38.story: For the comparison to be fair, the two families must be seen through the same veil, and they are. The dust in front of each dims and reddens their light by about the same amount, so the contrast in sparkle is a contrast in the stars themselves. Astronomers check this by comparing each member's color with the color its spectrum says it should have, and the excess redness measures the dust.

M39.beat: Thinning out: a family near the end of its cluster days
M39.question: Will M39 still be a cluster a few hundred million years from now?
M39.why: M39 is a nearby family about 430 million years old, close enough to count its brightest members one by one, and it has reached the age at which most families start to come apart.
M39.look: From Deneb sweep about nine degrees east-north-east to a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon. Count the members you can see at low power: they are spread wide, with no tight core.
M39.answer: M39 will probably have dissolved by then: with only about 500 Suns' worth of stars, its gravity is too weak to resist the galaxy's pull for ever. Its members will go on traveling side by side long after the cluster has gone, a family recognizable only by its shared motion.
M39.story: The end of a cluster is a slow unwinding rather than an explosion. Escaped members keep nearly the cluster's orbit around the galaxy, those slightly closer in pulling ahead and those slightly farther out falling behind, so the family stretches into a long thin stream along its path. After a few more laps the stream grows so long and faint that only careful measurements of motion can still trace it.

M41.beat: First to age: the orange giant
M41.question: Why does one star near M41's center glow orange among its white siblings?
M41.why: M41 sits just south of Sirius, a family of about a thousand stars, and one of them stands out from all the rest by its color.
M41.look: Put Sirius at the top of the field and move about four degrees straight south. M41 breaks into dozens of stars, and near its middle one has a clear orange tint; compare it with the white stars around it.
M41.answer: It was born with the rest but heavier, so it ran out of hydrogen in its core first and swelled into a cooler giant. Only the heaviest siblings have reached that point, which dates the family to about 150 million years, and the others will follow in order of their weight.
M41.story: A family's giants arrive in order of weight. The heaviest members swelled first and may already be gone, while the giant you see is a slightly lighter sibling caught in the act. The swollen stage is brief, a small fraction of a star's life, so a family of a thousand shows only a few giants at any one time, which is why a lone orange point near the middle is such a clear clock.

M44.beat: First to age: a clock that matches the Hyades
M44.question: Why does the Beehive's family clock read almost the same as the Hyades'?
M44.why: The Beehive is a family whose heaviest siblings are long gone and whose next heaviest are only now swelling into giants, one of the best-read clocks in the sky.
M44.look: Midway between Pollux and Regulus, let the cluster fill the field: dozens of white and pale-yellow stars, with a few warmer yellow-orange points among them, the siblings that have just begun to age.
M44.answer: The two may well be cousins. Both are about 600 to 700 million years old and move through space in a similar way, which has led astronomers to suggest they formed in the same great star-forming complex and have drifted apart since. If so, two families now separated by the whole width of Gemini once shared a birthplace.
M44.story: The case for kinship rests on more than age. The two families are unusually rich in heavy elements, matching each other closely and the Sun less well, and they share their motion through the galaxy with a loose stream of stars sometimes called the Hyades stream. Part of that stream turns out to be stars nudged into step by the galaxy's spiral arms rather than true siblings, which is why the cousin idea remains a hypothesis.

M45.question: How can anyone tell that the Seven Sisters really are sisters?
M45.why: The Pleiades are the sky's best-known star family, near enough that you can see its members one by one, so they set the standard every other family is measured against.
M45.look: Let the cluster fill the field: the bright members share one blue-white, and dozens of fainter stars gather around the little dipper rather than spreading evenly across the view.
M45.answer: They pass every test of kinship: Gaia counts more than 1,700 members, and the bright sisters and all the rest share one distance, one drift across the sky and one age. Their matching color is the visible part of it, since stars born on the same day differ mainly in mass, and mass is what time acts on first.
M45.story: A shared drift across the sky is only half of a family's motion; the other half, toward or away from us, is read from the Doppler shift of each star's spectral lines, and the Pleiades share that too. A chance passer-by might match one of these tests, but almost never all of them. Their spectra add a last check, since siblings from one cloud carry its recipe of elements down to small details that set one family apart from another.

M46.question: What does M46's soft glow say about how far its family has aged?
M46.why: M46 sits just east of the young, sparkling M47, an older family about three times farther away, which turns the two into a before-and-after pair.
M46.look: From M47 move just over a degree east to a soft, even glow with a few stars at the threshold. Under dark skies averted vision resolves more members, all of a similar faintness.
M46.answer: It says that the family's brightest days are behind it: at about 430 million years its hot blue members are gone, and the modest stars that remain are too faint at this distance to sparkle. With some 7,900 Suns' worth of stars, though, it is heavy enough to stay a family for a long time yet.
M46.story: Comparing the two fairly means correcting for distance first. Placed side by side at the same range, this family's brightest stars would still fall well short of its neighbor's, because its blue heavyweights have died and the top of the family now belongs to stars of a few Suns. Its softer look is partly distance, but mostly age.

M47.beat: Born together: a bright young family
M47.question: Why do M47's brightest stars all share the same icy blue-white?
M47.why: M47 is a young family close enough to show its members one by one, so it shows plainly what a family looks like while its brightest siblings are all still in their prime.
M47.look: Center the coarse scatter of bright stars, about the width of the full Moon. Its brightest members share one icy blue-white; then glance just over a degree east at M46, whose soft mist belongs to a different, older family.
M47.answer: They are siblings of one age, about 100 million years, and in a family that young a star's color follows its mass, so all the heaviest members glow hot together. None of them has yet used up its core hydrogen, which is exactly what the older family of M46 next door has had time to do.
M47.story: In a family still in its prime, every member sits on one line on a chart of color against brightness, the line of stars steadily burning hydrogen, and where a star sits on it is set almost entirely by its mass.
